107447.e: Scavenger cells are a kind of white blood cell. They take up bacteria and destroy them.

107448.q: Which blood cells protect the body from germs?
107448.e: White blood cells are the body’s defence cells. Some eat germs, others make antibodies.
107448.m: White blood cells are the police in the blood.

107449.q: Which blood cells are called erythrocytes in a blood count?
107449.e: The name comes from the Greek “erythros”, meaning red. In a blood count they are counted and their size is measured.
107449.m: Erythrocytes are the red blood cells.

107450.q: Where are new red blood cells made?
107450.e: Billions of new red blood cells are made in the bone marrow every day. They replace the old ones, which are broken down after about 120 days.
107450.m: Red blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

107451.e: Platelets are pieces pinched off from larger cells. That is why they have no nucleus of their own.

107452.q: Where in the body are platelets made?
107452.e: In the bone marrow, many small platelets are pinched off from large cells. The other blood cells are made there too.
107452.m: Platelets are made in the bone marrow.

107454.q: What happens if someone has too few platelets?
a: They bruise and bleed more easily
They get a fever straight away
They see less well at night
107454.e: Without enough platelets, the blood clots less well. Even small knocks then cause bruises, and wounds bleed for longer.
107454.m: Too few platelets lead to more bleeding.

107455.q: Roughly how long does a platelet live?
a: About a week to ten days
107455.e: Platelets have a short life of around a week. That is why the bone marrow constantly has to make new ones.
107455.m: Platelets only live for about a week.

107456.q: Which well-known medicine stops platelets working and is therefore used to help prevent heart attacks?
107456.e: Acetylsalicylic acid, known as aspirin, stops platelets from sticking together. In a small dose it can prevent blood clots in the vessels.
107456.m: Aspirin stops platelets from sticking together.

107457.q: In which organ are old platelets mainly broken down?
107457.e: The spleen filters aged blood cells out of the blood. Most old platelets are broken down there too.
107457.m: Old platelets are mainly broken down in the spleen.

a: A blood product made from donated platelets
A device for measuring blood pressure
A test to find out the blood group
107458.e: Platelet concentrates are given, for example, to people after chemotherapy who have too few platelets of their own. They help to prevent bleeding.
107458.m: A platelet concentrate contains donated platelets.

107459.q: What forms in a wound so that it stops bleeding?
107459.e: When you are injured, the blood clots. Fine threads of fibrin form a net, and a plug forms that closes the wound.

107460.q: Which small parts of the blood help fibrin to close a wound?
107460.e: Platelets gather at the wound and stick together. Together with the fibrin net, they form a firm plug.

107461.q: What shape does fibrin form in a wound?
107461.e: Fibrin threads join up into a dense net. Blood cells get caught in it, and a firm plug forms.
107461.m: Fibrin forms a net in which blood cells get caught.

107462.q: In which organ is fibrinogen made?
107462.e: The liver makes many plasma proteins, including fibrinogen and other clotting factors. That is why clotting can be disturbed in liver diseases.
107462.m: The liver makes many substances for blood clotting.

107463.q: What happens to the blood clot once the wound has healed?
107463.e: After healing, the body breaks down the fibrin net again. This process is called fibrinolysis.
107463.m: The body dissolves blood clots again after healing.

107465.q: What do surgeons use fibrin glue for?
a: To seal wounds and stop bleeding
107465.e: Fibrin glue copies the last step of blood clotting. It makes a firm clot form on the wound and sticks tissue together.
107465.m: Fibrin glue closes wounds like naturally clotted blood.

107466.q: Why can a small cut stop bleeding after a few minutes?
a: The blood clots and seals it
The heart stops beating for a moment
107466.e: When you are injured, the blood clots. Threads of fibrin form a net and seal the wound.

107467.q: What is the medical term for the bleeding disorder in which blood clots too slowly?
107467.e: In haemophilia, the blood clots too slowly. Even small injuries can therefore bleed for a long time.
107467.m: The medical name for this bleeding disorder is haemophilia.

107468.q: What does not work properly in haemophilia?
107468.e: In haemophilia, the blood clots too slowly. A wound therefore closes only poorly.
107468.m: In haemophilia, the blood clots poorly.

107469.q: What is missing in the blood of people with haemophilia?
107469.e: In haemophilia, a particular protein needed for blood clotting is missing. That is why bleeding is slow to stop.
107469.m: In haemophilia, a clotting substance is missing from the blood.

107470.q: Why do many more boys and men have haemophilia?
a: The gene is on the X chromosome
107470.e: Men have only one X chromosome. If the gene on it is changed, there is no second X to make up for the fault.
107470.m: Haemophilia is inherited via the X chromosome and mainly affects men.

107471.q: Why was haemophilia once called a disease of royal families?
a: It appeared in several European royal families
Only kings were allowed to treat it
You got it from wearing a crown
Only rich people could get it
107471.e: Britain's Queen Victoria carried the gene. Through her descendants, the disease reached the royal families of Spain, Russia and Prussia.
107471.m: Haemophilia spread through European royal families.

107472.q: Can you catch haemophilia from someone?
a: No, people are born with it
107472.e: Haemophilia is passed on through the genes. People have it from birth and cannot infect anyone.
107472.m: Haemophilia is present from birth and is not contagious.

107473.q: How is haemophilia mostly treated today?
a: With injections of the missing clotting factor
With lots of exercise in the sun
With a brace on the teeth
107473.e: People with haemophilia inject the missing factor into a vein regularly or when needed. This lets many of them lead an almost normal life.
107473.m: In haemophilia, the missing clotting factor is injected.

107474.q: Why must people with haemophilia be careful in sports with lots of falls?
a: Even small injuries can bleed for a long time
107474.e: Because the blood clots poorly, bruises can lead to heavy internal bleeding. Swimming or cycling with protection are often good choices.
107474.m: With haemophilia, even small injuries can bleed for a long time.

107475.q: Where does internal bleeding happen especially often in severe haemophilia?
107475.e: Bleeding into the knee, elbow and ankle joints is typical. Without treatment, the joints can be permanently damaged.
107475.m: In haemophilia, the joints often bleed.

107476.q: What does the word “leukaemia” literally mean?
107476.e: The word comes from Greek: “leukos” means white and “haima” means blood. In severe illness the blood can look paler.

107477.q: Which cells multiply out of control in leukaemia?
107477.e: In leukaemia, huge numbers of immature white blood cells are made. They cannot do their jobs and crowd out healthy blood cells.
107477.m: In leukaemia, immature white blood cells multiply out of control.

107478.q: Which type of cancer is most common in children?
107478.e: About a third of all cancers in children are leukaemias. Today most children can be cured.
107478.m: Leukaemia is the most common cancer in children.

107479.q: Why do people donate stem cells for leukaemia patients?
a: So the patients can make healthy blood again
107479.e: In some leukaemias, the diseased bone marrow is replaced. Healthy stem cells from a donor then make healthy blood cells again.
107479.m: Donated stem cells can help leukaemia patients.

107480.q: Which treatment do people with leukaemia receive most often?
107480.e: In chemotherapy, medicines destroy the cancer cells. Depending on the type, other treatments are added.
107480.m: Leukaemia is mostly treated with chemotherapy.

107481.q: Where in the body are the blood cells made that are diseased in leukaemia?
107481.e: Blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the soft inside of the bones. In leukaemia, too many immature white blood cells are made there.
107481.m: Leukaemia starts in the bone marrow.

107482.q: Why are people with leukaemia often pale and tired?
a: Because too few red blood cells are made
Because they get too much sun
Because their heart is too big
107482.e: The cancer cells crowd out the making of healthy blood cells. With too few red blood cells, less oxygen reaches the body.
107482.m: Leukaemia crowds out healthy blood cells and therefore makes people tired.

107483.q: Which leukaemia is most common in older adults in Europe?
107483.e: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, CLL for short, often develops slowly over years. It mainly occurs in people over 60.
107483.m: In older people, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is the most common.

107484.q: Which condition can a severe lack of iron cause?
107484.e: Without enough iron, the body cannot make enough haemoglobin. This leads to iron deficiency anaemia.
107484.m: A lack of iron can lead to anaemia.

107485.q: Which vitamin improves the absorption of iron from plant foods?
107485.e: Vitamin C helps the gut absorb iron from plants better. A glass of orange juice with lentils is therefore a good idea.
107485.m: Vitamin C helps the body absorb iron.

107486.q: Roughly how much iron does an adult's body contain?
107486.e: An adult has only around 3 to 5 grams of iron, about as much as in a small nail. Most of it is in haemoglobin.
107486.m: The body contains only a few grams of iron.

107487.q: Why do you often feel tired when you lack iron?
107487.e: Iron is part of the red blood pigment that carries oxygen. Without enough iron, muscles and brain get less oxygen.
107487.m: A lack of iron makes you tired because less oxygen is carried.

107488.q: Which of these plant foods contains a lot of iron?
107488.e: Pulses such as lentils are good plant sources of iron. Cucumbers and apples, on the other hand, contain little iron.
107488.m: Lentils are a good plant source of iron.

107489.q: Which animal food contains a lot of iron?
107489.e: Red meat such as beef contains a lot of iron that the body can absorb well. Butter, cream and honey contain hardly any iron.
107489.m: Red meat is a good source of iron.

107490.q: Which drink with a meal can reduce the absorption of iron?
107490.e: Tannins in black tea bind iron in the gut. So it is better not to drink it right with iron-rich meals.
107490.m: Black tea with a meal reduces iron absorption.

107491.q: What does the hormone insulin do in the blood?
107491.e: Insulin makes sure that sugar moves from the blood into the cells. This lowers the blood sugar level.

107493.q: Where does the blood get sugar from when you have not eaten for a long time?
107493.e: The liver stores sugar as a reserve. When you do not eat for a long time, it releases some into the blood so that blood sugar does not drop too low.
107493.m: The liver is the body's sugar store.

107494.q: What is the illness called in which blood sugar is permanently too high?
107494.e: In diabetes, insulin is missing or does not work well enough. So too much sugar stays in the blood.
107494.m: In diabetes mellitus, blood sugar is permanently too high.

107495.q: What helps quickly when blood sugar is too low?
a: Glucose tablets or a sugary drink
107495.e: When blood sugar is too low, the brain needs energy fast. Glucose or sugary drinks get into the blood quickly.
107495.m: Glucose helps quickly when blood sugar is too low.

107496.q: Why was the discovery of insulin in 1921 so important?
a: Since then diabetes can be treated
Since then broken bones can be healed
Since then there have been vaccines
Since then people can donate blood
107496.e: Before that, people with type 1 diabetes often died young. With insulin they can live well today.
107496.m: Thanks to insulin, diabetes can be treated.

107497.q: Where in the body is the pancreas, which makes insulin?
a: In the belly behind the stomach
In the head behind the eyes
In the neck next to the larynx
In the leg next to the knee
107497.e: The pancreas lies across the upper belly behind the stomach. It makes insulin and digestive juices.
107497.m: The pancreas lies behind the stomach.

107498.q: Which type of diabetes usually starts in childhood or the teenage years?
107498.e: In type 1 diabetes, the body's own immune system destroys the cells that make insulin. People with it need insulin for the rest of their lives.
107498.m: Type 1 diabetes often starts in children and teenagers.

107499.q: What do many people with diabetes use to check their own blood sugar?
a: A blood glucose meter or sensor
107499.e: A blood glucose meter measures the sugar in a drop of blood from the fingertip. Modern sensors on the skin measure all the time.
107499.m: People with diabetes often measure their blood sugar themselves.

107500.q: What did Karl Landsteiner observe when he mixed blood from different people?
107500.e: Landsteiner saw that some blood samples mix well and others clump together. This is how he discovered the blood groups.
107500.m: Blood that does not match clumps together.

107501.q: Which prize did Karl Landsteiner receive in 1930?
107501.e: For discovering the human blood groups, Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1930.
107501.m: Karl Landsteiner received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1930.

107502.q: Which international day takes place on Karl Landsteiner's birthday, 14 June?
107502.e: World Blood Donor Day honours Landsteiner, who was born on 14 June 1868. On this day, blood donors are thanked.
107502.m: World Blood Donor Day is on 14 June.

107503.q: What did Karl Landsteiner discover around the year 1900?
107503.e: Karl Landsteiner found out that people have different blood groups. He later received the Nobel Prize for this.
107503.m: Karl Landsteiner discovered the blood groups.

107504.q: Why is Landsteiner's discovery so important for blood transfusions?
a: Not all blood suits every person
107504.e: If someone receives blood of an unsuitable blood group, it can be life-threatening. Since Landsteiner, the blood group is checked before every transfusion.
107504.m: Before a blood transfusion, the blood group must match.

107505.q: Which further blood group feature did Landsteiner describe in 1940 together with Alexander Wiener?
107505.e: Together with Wiener, Landsteiner found an additional feature of red blood cells in 1940. This made transfusions even safer.
107505.m: Landsteiner also helped discover the rhesus factor.

107506.q: Which blood group exists besides A, B and AB?
107506.e: In Karl Landsteiner's system there are the blood groups A, B, AB and O. He first called group O “C”.
107506.m: The blood groups are A, B, AB and O.

107507.e: Landsteiner studied medicine in Vienna and worked as a doctor and researcher in pathology. He made his discoveries in the laboratory.
107507.m: Karl Landsteiner was a doctor and researcher.

107508.q: In which unit is buoyant force measured?
107508.e: Buoyancy is a force. Forces are measured in newtons, named after Isaac Newton.
107508.m: Buoyant force is measured in newtons.

107509.q: What does the buoyant force on a fully submerged object NOT depend on?
a: The acceleration due to gravity g
107509.e: Buoyancy depends only on the volume displaced, the density of the liquid and g. An iron ball and a wooden ball of the same size experience the same buoyancy under water.
107509.m: Objects of the same size experience the same buoyancy under water.

107510.q: Is there a buoyant force in air too?
a: Yes, in all liquids and gases
107510.e: Buoyancy occurs in every fluid, that is in liquids and gases. Because air is very light, the buoyancy there is usually small.
107510.m: There is buoyancy in liquids and in gases.

107511.q: Why is there a buoyant force in water?
a: The water pressure is greater at the bottom of the object than at the top
The water attracts the object magnetically
The object loses mass in water
107511.e: The pressure in water increases with depth. So the water pushes harder on the underside than on the top, leaving an upward force.
107511.m: Buoyancy occurs because water pressure increases with depth.

107512.q: An object with a volume of 0.5 dm³ is fully submerged in salt water with 1.2 kg per dm³. Roughly how great is the buoyancy (g equals 10 N/kg)?
107512.e: The displaced salt water has a mass of 0.5 dm³ times 1.2 kg/dm³, which is 0.6 kg. Times 10 N/kg, this gives 6 N.
107512.m: Buoyancy is equal to the weight of the displaced liquid.

107513.q: A force meter shows 8 N for a stone in air and 5 N in water. How great is the buoyancy?
107513.e: The difference between the two readings is the buoyancy: 8 N minus 5 N gives 3 N.
107513.m: Buoyancy is measured as the difference between the force in air and in water.

107514.q: An object fully submerged in water experiences a buoyancy of 15 N. What is its volume (g equals 10 N/kg)?
107514.e: 15 N equals the weight of 1.5 kg of water. 1.5 kg of water has a volume of 1.5 litres.
107514.m: You can calculate an object’s volume from its buoyancy in water.

107515.q: A stone is dipped first in water and then in cooking oil. Where is the buoyancy smaller?
a: There is no buoyancy in either
107515.e: Cooking oil has a lower density than water. The displaced oil is therefore lighter, and the buoyancy is smaller.
107515.m: The lower the density of the liquid, the smaller the buoyancy.

107516.q: Does the buoyancy of a solid stone change as it sinks deeper in a lake?
a: No, it stays practically the same
107516.e: The pressure does increase everywhere, but the pressure difference between the top and bottom stays the same. As long as the volume does not change, the buoyancy stays the same too.
107516.m: The buoyancy of a rigid object does not depend on how deep it is.

107517.q: How is buoyant force calculated according to Archimedes’ principle?
a: Density of the liquid times g times volume displaced
Mass of the object times speed
Volume of the object divided by its mass
107517.e: The buoyant force is the weight of the displaced liquid. This is calculated from the density, the volume and the acceleration due to gravity g.
107517.m: Buoyant force comes from the density of the liquid, g and the volume displaced.

107519.q: An aluminium cube has a volume of 1 dm³ and weighs 27 N. What does a force meter show when the cube hangs fully in water (g equals 10 N/kg)?
107519.e: The cube displaces 1 litre of water, which is 1 kg and therefore 10 N of buoyancy. 27 N minus 10 N gives 17 N.
107519.m: Under water, an object seems lighter by the amount of its buoyancy.

107520.q: A stone with a mass of 600 g displaces 200 ml of water in a measuring jug. What is its density?
107520.e: The 200 ml displaced corresponds to 200 cm³ of stone volume. 600 g divided by 200 cm³ gives 3 g/cm³.
107520.m: Water displacement can be used to find the volume and therefore the density.

107521.q: A block of wood has a density of 0.6 g/cm³. What part of its volume is under water when it floats?
107521.e: A floating object displaces as much water as it weighs. The ratio of the densities, 0.6 to 1, means that 60 per cent is under water.
107521.m: The part under water matches the ratio of the densities.

107522.q: Why does a very precise scale show slightly less for a large polystyrene block in air than in a vacuum?
a: The air produces a small buoyancy
The air reduces the block’s mass
The scale gets damp in the air
There is no gravity in a vacuum
107522.e: Air is displaced too and produces buoyancy. For large, light objects, this makes a measurable difference in precise measurements.
107522.m: Air also exerts a small buoyancy on objects.

107523.q: A ball with a volume of 2 dm³ is only half submerged in water. How great is the buoyancy (g equals 10 N/kg)?
107523.e: Only 1 dm³ is under water, so 1 kg of water is displaced. This gives 10 N of buoyancy.
107523.m: Only the submerged part of an object counts for buoyancy.

107524.q: A measuring device floats in a liquid and sinks deeper in light liquids. What does it measure?
107524.e: Such a hydrometer floats according to Archimedes’ principle. In liquids with a low density, it has to displace more and sinks deeper. The density is read off the scale.
107524.m: A hydrometer measures the density of a liquid.

107525.q: A cube with sides of 10 cm is fully submerged. How much water does it displace?
107525.e: The volume of the cube is 10 cm times 10 cm times 10 cm, which is 1000 cm³. This is exactly 1 litre of displaced water.
107525.m: A fully submerged object displaces its own volume of water.

107526.q: When does an object hover in water without rising or sinking?
a: When its density is the same as that of water
When it is smaller than a sugar cube
When it is made of metal
107526.e: With the same density, the weight is exactly as great as the buoyancy. Then the object stays put at any depth.
107526.m: An object hovers when its density matches that of water.

107527.q: When does an object sink in water?
a: When its weight is greater than the buoyancy
When its buoyancy is greater than its weight
107527.e: If the weight is greater than the buoyancy, a downward force remains. The object sinks to the bottom.
107527.m: An object sinks if it is heavier than the water it displaces.

107528.q: Roughly what share of an iceberg lies below the surface of the water?
107528.e: Ice has about 0.9 g/cm³, seawater around 1.03 g/cm³. This means that almost nine tenths of the iceberg lie under water.
107528.m: Most of an iceberg is hidden under water.

107529.e: Candle wax has a density of about 0.9 g/cm³ and is therefore lighter than water. Aluminium, glass and marble are denser and sink.
107529.m: Materials with a lower density than water float.

107530.q: Why does a Cartesian diver in a closed plastic bottle sink when you squeeze the bottle?
a: The air in the diver is squeezed, and water gets in
The pressure makes the water lighter
The hand makes the diver magnetic
107530.e: The pressure squeezes the air bubble in the diver. It displaces less water, becomes denser and sinks.
107530.m: A Cartesian diver sinks when its air bubble is squeezed.

107531.q: Why do you sink deeper in the swimming pool when you breathe out completely?
a: The body’s volume gets smaller, and so does the buoyancy
107531.e: With air in your lungs, your body has a larger volume. After breathing out, you displace less water and get less buoyancy.
107531.m: With full lungs, you float more easily.

107532.q: How great is the buoyancy of a floating boat compared with its weight?
107532.e: A floating object is in balance. The buoyancy exactly cancels out the weight, otherwise the boat would rise or sink.
107532.m: When something floats, the buoyancy equals the weight.

107533.q: A ball has a mass of 2 kg and a volume of 2.5 litres. What does it do in water?
a: It rises out of the water
107533.e: Its density is 2 kg divided by 2.5 litres, which is 0.8 kg per litre. That is less than water at 1 kg per litre.
107533.m: An object with a lower density than water floats.

107534.q: What does a ship’s displacement in tonnes tell you?
a: The mass of the displaced water and so the mass of the ship
107534.e: A floating ship displaces exactly as much water as it weighs. That is why the displacement tells you the mass of the ship.
107534.m: A ship’s displacement equals its mass.

107535.q: A ship has a mass of 500 tonnes. How much fresh water does it displace when it floats?
107535.e: The ship displaces 500 tonnes of water. One tonne of fresh water has a volume of one cubic metre, so it is 500 cubic metres.
107535.m: A ship displaces as much water as it weighs.

107536.q: A rowing boat displaces 0.3 cubic metres of lake water. What is the mass of the boat and crew together?
107536.e: 0.3 cubic metres of water is 300 litres and has a mass of 300 kg. That is exactly how much the boat and crew weigh.
107536.m: You can calculate the mass of a boat from the water it displaces.

107537.q: A cargo ship takes on 200 tonnes of cargo. By how much does its displacement increase?
107537.e: The ship becomes 200 tonnes heavier and sinks deeper. It then displaces exactly 200 tonnes more water.
107537.m: Every tonne of cargo increases the displacement by one tonne.

107538.q: What does a ship’s gross tonnage tell you?
a: The total internal volume of the ship
107538.e: Gross tonnage is a measure of the enclosed space of a ship. It is not a weight, even though people often loosely talk about tonnage.
107538.m: Gross tonnage describes the size of the ship’s interior.

107539.q: What is a boat called that always sits in the water and pushes it aside, unlike a planing boat?
107539.e: A displacement boat is carried by buoyancy at any speed. A planing boat partly lifts out of the water at high speed.
107539.m: A displacement boat is carried by buoyancy in the water.

107540.q: A stone lies in a boat on a pond. What happens to the water level of the pond if you throw the stone into the water?
107540.e: In the boat, the stone displaces water according to its mass, which is a large volume. On the bottom, it displaces only its own small volume, so the water level falls.
107540.m: A stone in a boat displaces more water than a stone on the bottom.

107541.q: An ice cube floats in a glass filled to the brim with water. What happens when it melts completely?
a: The water level stays the same
107541.e: The floating ice cube displaces exactly as much water as it weighs. Once melted, it fills exactly this volume.
107541.m: When floating ice melts, the water level stays the same.

107542.q: Why does a steel ship float, even though steel is much denser than water?
a: The hollow hull displaces a great deal of water
The engine keeps the ship up
The paint makes the steel lighter
107542.e: The hull encloses a lot of air. The whole ship therefore has an average density that is lower than that of water.
107542.m: A steel ship floats thanks to its hollow hull.

107543.q: What is the lowest lengthwise beam called that runs like a backbone through the whole hull of a ship?
107543.e: The keel is the most important part at the bottom of the hull. The ribs, or frames, rise upwards from it.
107543.m: The keel is the backbone of a ship’s hull.

107544.q: What is the front part of a ship’s hull called?
107544.e: The bow is the front end of a ship. The back end is called the stern.
107544.m: The bow is the front part of a ship.

107545.q: What does a ship’s draught describe?
a: How far the hull reaches below the waterline
How deep the sea is under the ship
How deep the ship can dive
How far you fall from the deck
107545.e: The draught is the vertical distance from the waterline to the lowest point of the hull. It decides which waters a ship can sail through.
107545.m: The draught shows how deep a ship sits in the water.

107546.q: Why do modern oil tankers have a double hull?
a: So that no oil leaks out if the outer hull is holed
So that they can take more passengers
107546.e: There is a gap between the outer and inner hull. If the outer hull is damaged, the oil stays in the inner hull.
107546.m: The double hull protects the sea from oil in tanker accidents.

107547.q: What is the rounded bulbous bow below the waterline of many large ships for?
a: It reduces water resistance and saves fuel
It is used as a battering ram
It is a window for divers
107547.e: The bulbous bow creates its own wave, which partly cancels out the bow wave. This means the ship needs less energy.
107547.m: A bulbous bow helps large ships to save fuel.

107548.q: How many hulls does a catamaran have?
107548.e: A catamaran consists of two slim hulls joined together. A boat with three hulls is called a trimaran.

107549.q: Why do bulkheads divide a ship’s hull into compartments?
a: So that the whole ship does not flood if there is a leak
So that the hull is lighter
So that the ship can turn faster
107549.e: Bulkheads are watertight dividing walls. If one compartment floods, the others stay dry and still provide buoyancy.
107549.m: Watertight bulkheads stop a damaged hull from flooding completely.

107550.q: Why must a ship not be loaded as heavily as you like?
a: It could sink in high waves
It would be blown away by the wind
107550.e: An overloaded ship sits low in the water. In a storm, waves break over the deck, and the ship can sink. That is why there is the load line mark.
107550.m: Overloaded ships are in danger in a storm.

107551.q: What does the load line mark on the side of a ship show?
a: The deepest the loaded ship may sit in the water
How fast the ship may sail
How many people are on board
107551.e: Depending on the waters and the season, the waterline must not go above a certain line. This keeps enough reserve above the water.
107551.m: The load line mark shows the maximum permitted loading.

107552.q: What is meant by a ship’s freeboard?
a: The distance from the waterline to the deck
The space for passengers without a ticket
The distance between two ships in the harbour
107552.e: The freeboard is the part of the ship’s side that sticks out of the water. The greater it is, the safer the ship is in waves.
107552.m: The freeboard is the distance between the waterline and the deck.

107553.q: Why is the fresh water mark on the load line mark higher than the one for seawater?
a: Because a ship sinks deeper in fresh water
Because fresh water has higher waves
Because rivers are deeper than the sea
107553.e: Fresh water has a lower density than seawater. The same ship must therefore displace more volume and sinks deeper.
107553.m: In fresh water, a ship sits lower than in the sea.

107554.q: What does the mark “W” on the load line mark stand for?
107554.e: In winter, the sea is often stormier. That is why a ship may then be loaded less deeply than in summer.
107554.m: The winter mark allows less loading than the summer mark.

107555.q: Why is the tropical mark on the load line mark higher than the summer mark?
a: Because the weather in tropical seas is usually calmer
Because ships sail more slowly in the tropics
Because there are no waves in the tropics
107555.e: In tropical waters, the weather outside the storm season is considered calmer. That is why a ship may be loaded a little deeper there.
107555.m: In the tropics, a ship may be loaded a little deeper.

107556.q: What happens to a ship when it is loaded more heavily?
a: It sinks deeper into the water
It rises out of the water
It stays at exactly the same depth
107556.e: A heavier ship has to displace more water for the buoyancy to carry it. That is why it sits deeper.
107556.m: The more heavily a ship is loaded, the lower it sits in the water.

107557.q: Who decides how deeply ships may be loaded on the world’s oceans?
107557.e: Since 1966, an international agreement has set the load lines. It applies to ships all over the world.

107558.q: Why do empty cargo ships take ballast water into tanks?
a: So that they sit stably in the water
So that the crew can shower
107558.e: An empty ship sits very high and can easily capsize. The ballast water makes it heavier and lowers its centre of gravity, and it also keeps the propeller under water.
107558.m: Ballast water makes empty ships more stable.

107559.q: What environmental problem can ships’ ballast water cause?
a: It carries foreign species to other seas
107559.e: Ships pump in ballast water in one port and pump it out again in another. Small animals and algae travel with the water and can spread as invasive species.
107559.m: Ballast water can bring foreign species to new areas.

107560.q: What must ships do with their ballast water today before releasing it?
a: Treat it so that no foreign organisms travel with it
Heat it first so that it evaporates
107560.e: Since 2017, there have been worldwide rules for ballast water. It is cleaned or exchanged on the high seas so that no foreign species spread.
107560.m: Today, ballast water must be treated.

107561.q: Why does a submarine have smaller trim tanks as well as the large ballast tanks?
a: To set its position and hovering exactly
107561.e: Small amounts of water are pumped back and forth between the trim tanks. This lets the submarine hover perfectly level at a particular depth.
107561.m: Trim tanks are used to fine-tune a submarine.

107562.q: A submerged submarine displaces 1200 t of water, and its mass without ballast water is 1000 t. How much water must it take in to hover?
107562.e: To hover, its mass must be the same as the mass of the displaced water. 1200 t minus 1000 t gives 200 t of ballast water.
107562.m: A submarine hovers when its mass equals the mass of the displaced water.

107563.q: Why do many sailing boats have heavy lead in the keel as ballast?
a: So that the low centre of gravity stops them capsizing
107563.e: The wind pushes the sail sideways and tries to tip the boat over. The heavy ballast low down rights the boat again.
107563.m: Ballast low in the keel keeps a sailing boat upright.

107564.q: How does a submarine surface again?
a: It forces the water out of the ballast tanks with compressed air
It lets more water into the ballast tanks
107564.e: When the water is forced out of the tanks, the submarine gets lighter. The buoyancy is then greater than the weight, and it rises.
107564.m: A submarine surfaces when it forces water out of its ballast tanks.

107565.q: What happens to a ship if a ballast tank on only one side is filled?
a: It lifts right out of the water
107565.e: The extra water makes one side heavier. By filling tanks in a targeted way, you can also correct a tilt caused by uneven cargo.
107565.m: Ballast tanks can be used to correct a ship’s tilt.

107566.q: What does the prefix “meso” in the word mesoscaphe mean?
107566.e: “Mesos” is Greek for middle. A mesoscaphe is a submersible for middle sea depths.
107566.m: A mesoscaphe is a submersible for middle depths.

107567.q: How does a mesoscaphe differ from a bathyscaphe?
a: It only dives to middle depths, not to the deep sea
107567.e: The bathyscaphe is built for the greatest depths. A mesoscaphe is more manoeuvrable and intended for middle depths of a few hundred metres.
107567.m: The mesoscaphe is built for middle depths, the bathyscaphe for the deep sea.

107568.q: Which Swiss man built the mesoscaphe for the Expo 64 national exhibition?
107568.e: Jacques Piccard carried out his father’s plans and built the tourist submarine. It was one of the main attractions of Expo 64 in Lausanne.
107568.m: Jacques Piccard built the mesoscaphe for Expo 64.

107569.q: What was special about the Expo 64 mesoscaphe?
a: It was the first submarine for tourists
It was built entirely of wood
107569.e: With the Expo 64 mesoscaphe, visitors could dive in a submarine as passengers for the very first time.
107569.m: The Expo 64 mesoscaphe was the first tourist submarine.

107570.q: In which lake did the mesoscaphe dive during Expo 64 in Lausanne?
107570.e: Expo 64 took place in Lausanne on Lake Geneva. The mesoscaphe made many dives there with visitors.
107570.m: The Expo 64 mesoscaphe dived in Lake Geneva.

107571.q: Which ocean current did Jacques Piccard explore in 1969 with the mesoscaphe “Ben Franklin”?
107571.e: The “Ben Franklin” drifted under water with the Gulf Stream off the east coast of the USA. The researchers measured temperature, currents and sea life.
107571.m: In 1969, Jacques Piccard drifted in the Gulf Stream in a mesoscaphe.

107572.q: Roughly how long did the underwater drift of the “Ben Franklin” in 1969 last?
107572.e: The crew stayed under water from 14 July to 14 August 1969. They drifted with the Gulf Stream from Florida to off the coast of Nova Scotia in Canada.
107572.m: The “Ben Franklin” stayed under water for about a month.

107573.q: Which space agency used the voyage of the “Ben Franklin” to study life in cramped spaces?
107573.e: NASA was interested in how a crew lives for weeks in a small space. The findings helped with the planning of space stations.
107573.m: NASA learned from the “Ben Franklin” for long space flights.

107574.q: What does the word “bathyscaphe” mean when translated?
107574.e: The word comes from Greek: “bathys” means deep, “skaphos” means ship.
107574.m: A bathyscaphe is literally a deep-sea ship.

107575.q: What was the large float of the Trieste filled with to produce buoyancy?
107575.e: Petrol is lighter than water and can hardly be compressed. That is why it reliably provided buoyancy even under enormous pressure.
107575.m: The Trieste got its buoyancy from a tank full of petrol.

107576.q: What did the Trieste release in order to rise again?
107576.e: The Trieste carried tonnes of small iron pellets in containers held by electromagnets. When the current was switched off, the ballast fell out and the vessel rose.
107576.m: The Trieste rose by dropping iron ballast.

107577.q: Which city is the Trieste named after?
107577.e: The city of Trieste and companies there gave major support to the building of the bathyscaphe. That is why it was given the city’s name in 1953.
107577.m: The Trieste bears the name of the Italian city of Trieste.

107578.q: What did the Trieste achieve in 1960?
a: It dived to the deepest point of the oceans
It was the first ship to sail round the world
107578.e: In 1960, the Trieste dived almost 11 km deep into the Mariana Trench with two men on board. That is the deepest place in the oceans.
107578.m: In 1960, the Trieste reached the bottom of the Mariana Trench.

107579.q: Where did the crew of the Trieste sit?
a: In a steel sphere under the float
107579.e: The crew sat in a thick-walled pressure sphere made of steel. It hung under the large float.
107579.m: The crew of the Trieste sat in a steel pressure sphere.

107580.q: Why did the crew sphere of the Trieste have only one small, very thick window?
a: So that it could withstand the enormous water pressure
So that no light got in
So that the fish could not look in
So that it was easier to clean
107580.e: In the deep sea, water presses on every surface with enormous force. A small, thick window withstands this pressure much better than a large one.
107580.m: Deep-sea windows are small and thick because of the water pressure.

107581.q: Roughly how long did the Trieste’s descent to the bottom of the Mariana Trench take in 1960?
107581.e: The Trieste sank almost 11 kilometres at a steady speed. The descent took almost five hours.
107581.m: The Trieste’s descent into the deep sea took about five hours.

107582.q: Why did the Trieste not rise like a submarine by blowing out tanks with compressed air?
a: The water pressure in the deep sea would be far too great for this
Compressed air was banned at that time
107582.e: At a depth of almost 11,000 m, the pressure is over 1000 bar. Compressed air could hardly force water out of tanks there, so the Trieste dropped solid ballast.
107582.m: In the deep sea, compressed air does not help you to surface.

107583.q: Roughly how salty is the Dead Sea?
107583.e: The Dead Sea contains about ten times as much salt as the oceans, which have about 3.5 per cent. It is one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth.
107583.m: The Dead Sea is about ten times saltier than the sea.

107584.q: Where is the shore of the Dead Sea compared with sea level?
107584.e: The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest point on land on Earth. It lies more than 400 metres below sea level.
107584.m: The Dead Sea lies lower than any other shore in the world.

107585.q: Which river is the most important river flowing into the Dead Sea?
107585.e: The Jordan flows south from the Sea of Galilee into the Dead Sea. Today, it carries much less water than before because water is taken from it.
107585.m: The Jordan flows into the Dead Sea.

107586.q: Why is the Dead Sea so salty?
a: It has no outflow, and the water evaporates
Salt is added to it every day
It is connected to the ocean
107586.e: The water of the Dead Sea can only evaporate. The salt stays behind and builds up over a long time.
107586.m: A lake without an outflow gets saltier and saltier through evaporation.

107587.q: Why can you float so easily on the surface of the Dead Sea?
a: The salty water has a high density
The water there is especially warm
The water contains a lot of air
107587.e: A great deal of salt is dissolved in the water of the Dead Sea. It is therefore much denser than fresh water and gives more buoyancy.
107587.m: The water of the Dead Sea is much denser than fresh water.

107588.q: Which country lies on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea?
107588.e: The border runs right through the middle of the Dead Sea. Jordan lies on the eastern side.
107588.m: Jordan lies on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea.

107589.q: An object with a volume of 60 litres is fully submerged in the Dead Sea at 1.24 kg per litre. How great is the buoyancy (g equals 10 N/kg)?
107589.e: The displaced water has a mass of 60 times 1.24 kg, which is 74.4 kg. Times 10 N/kg, this gives 744 N.
107589.m: In the Dead Sea, the buoyancy is greater than in fresh water.

107590.q: What is a fish’s swim bladder filled with?
107590.e: The swim bladder contains a mixture of gases, mainly oxygen, nitrogen and carbon dioxide. When the fish changes the amount of gas, its volume changes.
107590.m: A fish’s swim bladder is filled with gas.

107591.q: How do sharks without a swim bladder stop themselves from sinking too fast?
a: With a balloon in their stomach
107591.e: A shark’s liver contains a lot of oil, which is lighter than water. In addition, the pectoral fins produce dynamic lift when swimming.
107591.m: Sharks use an oily liver instead of a swim bladder.

107592.q: In terms of evolution, which organ of land vertebrates is the swim bladder related to?
107592.e: The swim bladder and the lungs both come from a shared outgrowth of the gut. In some fish, such as the lungfish, it is even used for breathing.
107592.m: The swim bladder and the lungs have a common origin.

107593.q: What advantage does the swim bladder give a fish?
a: It can hover at one depth without effort
It can walk on land with it
It can produce light with it
It can poison prey with it
107593.e: With the right amount of gas, the fish has the same density as the water. This saves energy, because it does not have to keep swimming to stay at the same height.
107593.m: Thanks to its swim bladder, a fish saves energy while hovering.

107594.q: What happens to the swim bladder if a fish is pulled up very quickly from great depth?
a: It shrinks to the size of a pea
It becomes as hard as stone
107594.e: As the depth decreases, the water pressure falls and the gas expands. If the fish cannot release the gas quickly enough, it is injured.
107594.m: During a fast ascent, the gas in the swim bladder expands.

107595.q: What else do fish of the carp family use their swim bladder for?
107595.e: In the carp family, tiny bones called the Weberian apparatus connect the swim bladder to the inner ear. The bladder acts like an amplifier for sound.
107595.m: Fish of the carp family hear better with the help of their swim bladder.

107596.q: How do fish with a connection between the swim bladder and the gut, such as carp, fill their swim bladder?
a: They gulp air at the surface
They eat air bubbles from plants
They make gas only from their food
107596.e: In these fish, a duct leads from the swim bladder to the gut. Through it, they can take in air or release gas.
107596.m: Carp can gulp air to fill their swim bladder.

107597.q: Why do adult flatfish such as the plaice have no swim bladder?
a: Because they live on the seabed
Because they only live in fresh water
107597.e: Flatfish usually lie flat on the bottom. They need no buoyancy there, and without a swim bladder they stay down more easily.
107597.m: Bottom-dwelling fish such as the plaice need no swim bladder.

107598.q: Which gas is lighter than air and, unlike hydrogen, does not burn?
107598.e: Helium is a noble gas and hardly reacts with other substances at all. That is why it is much safer than hydrogen for balloons.
107598.m: Helium is light and does not burn.

107599.q: Which gas was used to fill gas balloons in the past, even though it burns easily?
107599.e: Hydrogen is the lightest gas and gives a lot of buoyancy. Because it burns, helium is mostly used today.
107599.m: Hydrogen is very light but flammable.

107600.q: What does the crew of a gas balloon throw out to rise higher?
107600.e: Sandbags on board make the balloon heavier. When sand is thrown out, the buoyancy wins and the balloon rises.
107600.m: A gas balloon rises when ballast is thrown out.

107601.q: How do you make a gas balloon sink?
a: You let gas out through a valve
You heat the gas with a burner
107601.e: Some of the gas escapes through the valve. The balloon displaces less air, loses buoyancy and sinks.
107601.m: A gas balloon sinks when gas is let out.

107602.q: Why does a balloon filled with helium rise into the air?
a: Helium is attracted by the Sun
107602.e: The balloon displaces air that is heavier than the helium inside it. This creates a buoyancy that carries it upwards.
107602.m: A gas balloon rises because its gas is lighter than air.

107603.q: What makes a gas balloon different from a hot-air balloon?
a: It is filled with a light gas instead of hot air
107603.e: A gas balloon is filled with helium or hydrogen. A hot-air balloon rises because a burner heats the air in the envelope.
107603.m: Gas balloons fly with gas, hot-air balloons with warm air.

107604.q: Which Swiss man, together with Brian Jones, was the first to fly non-stop round the world in a balloon in 1999?
107604.e: Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones flew round the world in the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3 in just under 20 days. Later, Piccard also flew round the Earth in the solar plane Solar Impulse.
107604.m: In 1999, Bertrand Piccard flew round the world in a balloon.

107605.q: Why does the envelope of a gas balloon expand as it rises?
a: Because air pressure decreases with height
Because the Sun melts the gas
Because the wind blows into it
107605.e: The higher the balloon rises, the less air presses from outside. The gas inside therefore expands.
107605.m: At great height, the gas in the balloon expands.

107606.q: Roughly how much mass can one cubic metre of helium carry near the ground?
107606.e: One cubic metre of air weighs about 1.2 kg, one cubic metre of helium only about 0.18 kg. The balloon can carry the difference of about 1 kg.
107606.m: One cubic metre of helium can carry about one kilogram.

107607.q: What do spore plants such as ferns and mosses never form?
107607.e: Spore plants reproduce with spores instead of seeds. They do not form flowers. They are also called cryptogams.
107607.m: Spore plants have no flowers and no seeds.

107608.q: What is the basic difference between a spore and a seed?
a: It usually consists of only one cell
It always has a hard fruit case
It forms only in a flower
107608.e: A seed contains a small embryo and food tissue. A spore is usually just a single cell with a protective wall.
107608.m: A spore is built much more simply than a seed.

107609.q: Which of these plant groups does NOT belong to the spore plants?
107609.e: Conifers form seeds in cones and belong to the seed plants. Clubmosses, horsetails and mosses reproduce with spores.
107609.m: Conifers are seed plants, not spore plants.

107610.q: What are ferns, horsetails and clubmosses called together?
107610.e: Ferns, horsetails and clubmosses together form the pteridophytes. Unlike mosses, they have vascular bundles, but they have no seeds.
107610.m: Ferns, horsetails and clubmosses belong to the pteridophytes.

107611.q: How long ago did the first plants begin to colonise dry land?
107611.e: The first land plants were moss-like spore plants and appeared in the Palaeozoic era over 400 million years ago. Flowering plants came much later.
107611.m: The first land plants were spore plants.

107612.q: Why are spores still found in rocks after millions of years?
a: They keep growing in the rock
They are formed anew every year
107612.e: The outer wall of spores is made of sporopollenin, one of the most durable natural substances of all. That is why spores last a very long time.
107612.m: Spores are protected by a very stable wall.

107613.q: Why are fungi no longer counted as plants today, even though they form spores?
a: They form a kingdom of their own
107613.e: Fungi have no chlorophyll and feed on other substances. That is why they form a kingdom of their own alongside plants and animals.
107613.m: Fungi are neither plants nor animals.

107614.q: Which spore plant often grows across the forest floor with long, creeping shoots?
107614.e: The stag's-horn clubmoss forms creeping shoots metres long with small leaves on the ground. Clubmosses are protected in many areas.
107614.m: Clubmosses creep across the forest floor with long shoots.

107615.q: What is meant by alternation of generations in mosses and ferns?
a: A spore-forming and a sex-cell-forming generation take turns
Old plants die off completely every winter
Young plants always grow in the shade of the old ones
The plants change where they grow every year
107615.e: From a spore grows a generation that forms sex cells. From the fertilised egg cell grows a generation that forms spores again.
107615.m: In alternation of generations, two different generations follow one another.

107616.q: Where does a fern form its spores?
a: In brown clusters on the underside of the fronds
107616.e: Small brown clusters sit on the underside of fern fronds. The spores form inside them and are spread by the wind.
107616.m: Ferns form their spores on the underside of the fronds.

107617.q: What grows from a spore in a fern?
a: Straight away a large fern with fronds
107617.e: From the spore, a tiny, usually heart-shaped prothallus grows first. The sex cells form on it, and from them a new fern later grows.
107617.m: From a fern spore, a prothallus grows first.

107618.q: Which generation is the green moss plant you see in the forest?
107618.e: In mosses, the green plant is the generation with the sex cells. The spore capsule on its stalk is the other generation.
107618.m: In mosses, the green plant is the generation with the sex cells.

107619.q: Which generation is the large plant with fronds in ferns?
107619.e: In ferns it is the other way round from mosses. The eye-catching plant with fronds forms spores, while the generation with the sex cells is only tiny.
107619.m: In ferns, the large plant is the spore-forming generation.

107620.q: In true mosses, what does the stalk with the spore capsule feed on?
a: The green moss plant it sits on
107620.e: The spore capsule with its stalk grows on the moss plant and is supplied with nutrients by it. So it is not independent.
107620.m: The spore capsule of mosses lives on the green moss plant.

107621.q: How do mosses and ferns reproduce, since they have no flowers?
107621.e: Mosses and ferns form no flowers and no seeds. They spread with tiny spores that the wind carries away.
107621.m: Mosses and ferns reproduce with spores.

107622.q: In ferns, what grows from the fertilised egg cell?
a: A young fern plant with fronds
A spore capsule on a stalk
A small bulb in the ground
107622.e: The fertilised egg cell first develops on the prothallus. From it grows a young fern plant, which later forms spores itself.
107622.m: In ferns, a new fern plant grows from the fertilised egg cell.

107623.q: What do mosses and ferns need for fertilisation to work?
a: Water, for example rain or dew
Lots of sun and dry weather
107623.e: The male sex cells of mosses and ferns swim to the egg cell. For this they need a film of water, which is why these plants often grow in damp places.
107623.m: Mosses and ferns need water for fertilisation.

107624.q: What grows first out of a fern spore?
a: Straight away a large fern frond
107624.e: From the spore, a tiny green plate grows first, the prothallus. Only later does the young fern plant with fronds grow from it.
107624.m: From a fern spore, a prothallus grows first.

107625.q: In mosses, what grows first from a spore?
a: A fine green network of threads
107625.e: From the moss spore, a branched green network of threads grows first. Only from this do the small moss plants grow.
107625.m: In mosses, a green network of threads grows first from the spore.

107626.q: What shape is the prothallus of many ferns?
107626.e: The prothallus of many ferns is a flat, green, heart-shaped plate. It lies close to the damp ground.
107626.m: The fern prothallus is often a small, heart-shaped plate.

107627.q: How big is the prothallus of a fern usually?
a: As big as the palm of a hand
107627.e: The prothallus is usually only a few millimetres to about one centimetre across. That is why it is easily overlooked in nature.
107627.m: The prothallus of a fern is tiny.

107628.q: Why do ferns need moisture to reproduce?
a: The male sex cells swim through water to the egg cell
The spores only sprout at the bottom of lakes
The fronds only flower in the rain
The roots need water for the seeds
107628.e: Egg cells and moving male sex cells form on the prothallus. The male cells swim through a thin film of water to the egg cell.
107628.m: Ferns need a film of water for fertilisation.

107630.q: What happens to the prothallus when the young fern plant has its own leaves and roots?
a: It turns woody and becomes a trunk
107630.e: The prothallus only supplies the young fern plant at the beginning. As soon as the fern is independent, the prothallus dies.
107630.m: The prothallus dies as soon as the young fern is independent.

107631.q: How does the prothallus of a fern feed itself?
a: It carries out photosynthesis with chlorophyll
It lives only on the spore's food reserves
107631.e: The prothallus is green and can make its own sugar using light. So it is a small independent plant.
107631.m: The fern prothallus feeds itself through photosynthesis.

a: A container in which spores form
A root hair that takes in water
A pore through which air flows
A store for starch in the trunk
107632.e: Sporangia are small capsules in which spores are formed. When a capsule is ripe, it opens and releases the spores.

107633.q: What is inside the brown clusters on the underside of a fern frond?
107633.e: The brown clusters are made up of many sporangia. Large numbers of spores form in each of them.
107633.m: The brown clusters under fern fronds contain spores.

107634.q: How are a fern's spores usually spread?
107634.e: Fern spores are tiny and as light as dust. The wind carries them far away.

107635.q: What happens when a ripe fern sporangium dries out?
a: It splits open and flings the spores away
It falls to the ground as a seed
It turns green and keeps growing
It sucks water from the air
107635.e: A ring of special cells, the annulus, tightens as it dries. Suddenly the capsule splits open and the spores are flung away.
107635.m: Drying fern sporangia fling their spores away.

107636.q: Where does a fern spore sprout best?
107636.e: Ferns need water to sprout and to reproduce. That is why they grow mainly in damp, shady places.
107636.m: Fern spores sprout in damp, shady places.

107637.q: Why does a fern produce such an enormous number of spores?
a: Only a few land in a good place
So that its leaves turn brown
107637.e: Most spores land in places where they cannot sprout. The more spores a fern produces, the more likely it is that a new fern grows somewhere.
107637.m: Lots of spores increase the chance of new ferns.

a: As big as grains of rice
107638.e: Fern spores are only a fraction of a millimetre in size. You can only see single ones under a microscope.
107638.m: Fern spores are as tiny as dust.

107639.q: Where are the sporangia of a horsetail?
a: In a cone-like spike at the tip of the shoot
On the underside of broad fronds
107639.e: Horsetails carry their sporangia on shield-shaped scales. These are packed tightly in a cone-like spike at the tip of the shoot.
107639.m: Horsetails form their spores in a spike at the tip of the shoot.

107640.q: Where do liverworts get their name from?
a: The lobed shape of some species looks like a liver
They grow only on animal livers
They form cushions the size of a liver
107640.e: Some liverworts have a flat, lobed body that looks like a liver. That is why people used to believe they helped against liver complaints.
107640.m: Liverworts owe their name to their liver-like shape.

107641.q: Which liverwort with a flat, lobed body often grows on damp walls and in plant nurseries?
107641.e: The common liverwort forms flat, green lobes on damp ground. In plant nurseries, it often grows on the soil in flowerpots.
107641.m: The common liverwort likes to grow in damp places.

107642.q: Where do liverworts like to grow best?
107642.e: Liverworts dry out easily. You find them on stream banks, on damp soil and on wet walls.

107643.q: What are the small cups on the surface of the common liverwort for?
a: They contain small buds for reproduction
They collect dew as drinking water
107643.e: Tiny buds (gemmae) lie in the cups. Raindrops splash them out, and new plants grow from them.
107643.m: The common liverwort also reproduces with small buds from little cups.

107644.q: What do liverworts, like all mosses, not have?
107644.e: Mosses have no real roots. They hold on with fine threads and take in water over their whole surface.

107645.q: Apart from small buds, how do liverworts reproduce?
107645.e: Liverworts form spores in small capsules. New moss plants grow from them.

107646.q: What do the structures that carry the reproductive organs of the common liverwort look like?
a: Like round berries on the ground
107646.e: In the common liverwort, little umbrellas on stalks grow upwards. The organs with the sex cells sit on them.
107646.m: The common liverwort carries little umbrellas on stalks.

107647.q: Which two growth forms are distinguished among liverworts?
107647.e: Thalloid liverworts have a flat body. Leafy liverworts, with small stems and tiny leaves, look like true mosses.
107647.m: There are flat and leafy liverworts.

107648.q: What does a true moss form in its capsule to reproduce?
107648.e: Mosses never flower and form no seeds. Tiny spores form in the small capsule and are spread by the wind.

107649.q: Why is a cushion of moss so useful for the forest?
a: It soaks up water like a sponge
It keeps the trees warm in winter
107649.e: Moss cushions take up rainwater and release it slowly. That way the forest floor stays damp.
107649.m: Mosses store water like a sponge.

107650.q: Where does the haircap moss get its name from?
a: From the hairy cap over the spore capsule
From its smell of hair tonic
107650.e: In haircap moss, the cap over the capsule is densely covered with fine hairs. This reminded people of hair and gave the plant its name.
107650.m: Haircap moss has a hairy cap on its capsule.

107651.q: How thick are the tiny leaves of most true mosses?
a: As thick as a beech leaf
107651.e: Most moss leaves consist of just a single layer of cells. That is why they can take in water directly, but they also dry out quickly.
107651.m: Moss leaves are usually only one layer of cells thick.

107652.q: How do true mosses hold on to the ground or to stones?
107652.e: Mosses have no real roots. They anchor themselves with fine threads called rhizoids.
107652.m: Mosses hold on with fine anchoring threads.

107653.q: Why does the spore capsule of many true mosses stand on a long stalk?
a: So that the wind can spread the spores far
So that slugs can eat the capsule
So that the capsule stays in the ground
So that the moss can climb higher
107653.e: The stalk lifts the capsule above the moss cushion. Up there, the wind catches the spores more easily and carries them away.
107653.m: The long stalk helps to spread the spores.

107654.q: About how many species of moss are found in Switzerland?
107654.e: Over 1,000 species of true mosses, liverworts and hornworts are known in Switzerland. Because of the many habitats from the lowlands to the high mountains, the variety is great.
107654.m: Switzerland has a great variety of mosses.

107655.q: Why do mosses often grow in shady places, for example on the north side of trees?
a: It stays damp for longer there
The sun shines most strongly there
107655.e: Mosses dry out quickly and need moisture. In shady places, water evaporates more slowly.

107656.q: What is the living together of fungus and alga in a lichen called, from which both benefit?
107656.e: In a symbiosis, both partners gain an advantage. Together, fungus and alga form a new, shared living thing.
107656.m: A lichen is a symbiosis of fungus and alga.

107657.q: What does the fungus offer the alga in a lichen?
a: Protection from drying out and water with minerals
Light from its own glowing cells
107657.e: The fungal network wraps around the algal cells, holds on to moisture and takes up minerals. That way the algae can live even in barren places.
107657.m: In a lichen, the fungus protects the alga.

107658.q: What do many lichens on tree trunks tell us about the surroundings?
a: That the soil is rich in lime
107658.e: Many lichens react sensitively to air pollutants. Where many different lichens grow, the air is usually clean.
107658.m: Lichens are indicators of clean air.

107659.q: What does the alga supply to the fungus in a lichen?
107659.e: The alga makes sugar using sunlight. The fungus lives on it too, and in return protects the alga and supplies it with water.
107659.m: In a lichen, the alga feeds the fungus with sugar.

107660.q: How fast do most lichens grow?
a: Very slowly, often only millimetres a year
107660.e: Lichens grow very slowly. Some grow only a millimetre or less a year, but in return they can live to a great age.

107661.q: What are lichens called that are so firmly grown onto stone that you cannot remove them?
107661.e: Crustose lichens form a thin coating directly on stone or bark. The map lichen is an example.
107661.m: Crustose lichens are firmly grown onto their surface.

107662.q: Which growth form does tree lungwort, with its large, leaf-like lobes, belong to?
107662.e: Foliose lichens have leaf-like lobes that are attached to the surface only in places. Tree lungwort grows mainly in old, damp forests.

107663.q: Why are lichens called pioneer organisms?
a: They settle on bare rock and help to form soil
They were the first living things on Earth
They move to new areas every year
They are the first plants sown in a garden
107663.e: Lichens grow on bare rock and slowly dissolve it with acids. Their remains form a first thin layer of soil for other plants.
107663.m: On bare rock, lichens prepare the ground for other plants.

107664.q: What did experiments show in which lichens were taken into space on a satellite?
a: Some survived about two weeks in open space
All died after just a few seconds
They grew much faster in space
107664.e: In an experiment by the European Space Agency in 2005, lichens survived about two weeks of vacuum, cold and strong radiation. Afterwards they were active again.
107664.m: Some lichens can even survive in space.

107665.q: Which animal in the far north mainly eats lichens in winter?
107665.e: In winter, reindeer scrape away the snow and eat lichens, especially reindeer lichen. It is one of their most important sources of food there.
107665.m: In winter, reindeer live mainly on lichens.

107666.q: What do researchers use the slow growth of the map lichen for, for example in front of glaciers in the Alps?
a: To estimate how long a rock has been free of ice
To measure the height of the mountain
To find the direction of the North Pole
To predict when it will snow
107666.e: The map lichen grows very evenly and slowly. From the diameter of large lichens, you can estimate when a glacier uncovered the rock.
107666.m: Lichens can show the age of rock surfaces like a clock.

107667.q: What are living things called from which you can read the state of the environment?
107667.e: Bioindicators react sensitively to certain environmental conditions. Whether they are present or absent tells us something about the air, water or soil.
107667.m: Bioindicators show the state of the environment.

107668.q: To which air pollutant do many lichens react particularly sensitively?
107668.e: Sulphur dioxide is produced mainly when coal and heating oil are burnt. It damages the algae in the lichen, so many species die.
107668.m: Sulphur dioxide in the air harms many lichens.

107669.q: Why do lichens react so sensitively to pollutants in the air?
a: They take in water and substances over their whole surface
107669.e: Lichens have no roots and no protective waxy layer. They soak up rain and fog directly and so also build up pollutants.
107669.m: Lichens take in pollutants directly from the air and rain.

107670.q: What were urban areas called in the past where hardly any lichens grew because of dirty air?
107670.e: In industrial towns there used to be zones where hardly a single lichen survived on trees. These areas were called lichen deserts.
107670.m: A lichen desert shows heavily polluted air.

107671.q: Where does the bright yellow common orange lichen grow particularly often?
a: Only in very clean mountain air
107671.e: The common orange lichen likes a lot of nitrogen, such as gets into the air from farming and traffic. That is why it often grows on trees and walls near cowsheds and roads.
107671.m: The common orange lichen shows a lot of nitrogen in the air.

107672.q: Which growth form of lichens is considered particularly sensitive to air pollution?
107672.e: Fruticose lichens such as beard lichens have a large surface and react very sensitively. Crustose lichens are usually the toughest.
107672.m: Beard lichens grow only in clean air.

107673.q: What is the method called in which lichens on tree bark are recorded to assess air quality?
107673.e: In lichen mapping, you count on many trees which lichen species occur and how often. From this, a map of air quality is made.
107673.m: Lichen mapping can be used to assess air quality.

107674.q: Why do more lichens grow again in many Swiss towns today than 50 years ago?
a: Exhaust from heating systems and factories has become cleaner
The trees in the towns have become smaller
It rains much less today than in the past
Lichens are planted on purpose in parks
107674.e: Since coal and sulphur-rich heating oil are hardly used any more and exhaust gases are cleaned, the air is cleaner. Many sensitive lichens are therefore returning.
107674.m: Clean air lets lichens return to towns.

107675.q: Which species is the largest native horsetail?
107675.e: The great horsetail can grow over a metre tall. This makes it the largest horsetail in Europe.
107675.m: The great horsetail is the largest horsetail in Europe.

107676.q: With its many side branches, what does a horsetail look like?
107676.e: In the great horsetail, many thin green branches stand in rings around the stem. This makes it look like a little fir tree.
107676.m: A horsetail looks like a small fir tree.

107677.q: Where does the great horsetail typically grow?
a: On wet, lime-rich slopes with springs and on stream banks
In dry sand dunes by the sea
In the shade of dense conifer forests on sand
107677.e: The great horsetail needs a lot of water and lime-rich soil. You find it at springs, on wet slopes and by streams.
107677.m: The great horsetail loves wet, lime-rich soils.

107678.q: Which substance makes the stems of horsetails rough and hard?
107678.e: Horsetails store a lot of silica in their cell walls. This silicon compound makes them as rough as fine sandpaper.

107679.q: What do the brownish spring shoots of the great horsetail, which carry the spores, lack?
107679.e: The fertile shoots in spring are pale to brownish and have no chlorophyll. They live on reserves from the rootstock and die after the spores ripen.
107679.m: The spore shoots of the great horsetail have no chlorophyll.

107680.q: How are the leaves of horsetails built?
a: As small teeth joined to form a sheath
107680.e: The leaves of horsetails are greatly reduced. At each stem joint they form a toothed sheath; photosynthesis is mainly done by the green stem.
107680.m: In horsetails, the leaves are joined to form small sheaths.

107681.q: What nickname do horsetails have because of their bushy look?
107681.e: The scientific name Equisetum means horse's tail. The bushy shoots look like a horse's tail.
107681.m: Horsetails get their name from a horse's tail.

107682.e: Horsetails form no flowers and no seeds. Like ferns and mosses, they reproduce with tiny spores that the wind spreads.

107683.q: Where do tree ferns mainly grow today?
a: In tropical and subtropical mountain forests
In the high Alps above 3,000 metres
107683.e: Tree ferns love damp, mild areas, especially tropical mountain and cloud forests. They are also common in New Zealand and Australia.
107683.m: Tree ferns grow mainly in damp, warm mountain forests.

107684.q: How tall can the largest tree ferns grow?
107684.e: The largest tree ferns reach heights of about 20 metres. This makes them the largest ferns living today.
107684.m: Tree ferns can grow as tall as a house.

107685.q: What is the trunk of a tree fern made of?
a: An upright rootstock wrapped in many roots
Hard wood with bark, like an oak
107685.e: The trunk is an upright-growing rootstock without real wood. Towards the bottom it gets thicker and thicker because of a dense coat of roots.
107685.m: A tree fern has no real wooden trunk.

107686.q: Which tree fern is a well-known national symbol of New Zealand?
107686.e: The silver fern has fronds with a silvery-white underside. It appears on New Zealand's sports shirts, coins and coat of arms.
107686.m: The silver fern is a symbol of New Zealand.

107687.q: Why must a tree fern in a tub be protected in winter in Switzerland?
a: It comes from mild areas and does not cope well with hard frost
It needs a lot of fertiliser in winter
It flowers only in the snow
107687.e: Tree ferns such as Dicksonia antarctica come from damp, mild parts of Australia. Hard frost harms them.
107687.m: Tree ferns like it mild and damp.

107688.q: Why is the trade in many tree ferns restricted?
a: Too many were dug up for gardens
107688.e: Many tree ferns were over-harvested for the garden trade. That is why trade in them is restricted by the Washington Convention on endangered species (CITES).
107688.m: Trade in tree ferns is controlled internationally.

107689.q: Does the trunk of a tree fern form growth rings?
a: No, it does not grow thicker like wood
107689.e: Ferns have no growth layer that forms new wood every year. That is why there are no growth rings in a tree fern trunk.
107689.m: Tree ferns have no growth rings.

107690.q: Where do new fronds grow on a tree fern?
a: As a tuft at the top of the trunk
From the side of the lower trunk
From the roots next to the trunk
107690.e: Tree ferns usually have no branches. All the fronds grow together from the top of the trunk and form a crown, like a palm tree.
107690.m: On a tree fern, all the fronds grow at the top of the trunk.

107691.q: Which group of living things does reindeer lichen belong to, even though it is often called “reindeer moss”?
107691.e: Reindeer lichen is a partnership of fungus and alga. The name “reindeer moss” is misleading, because it is not related to mosses.
107691.m: Reindeer moss is really a lichen.

107692.q: What growth form does reindeer lichen have?
107692.e: Reindeer lichen forms small, densely branched tufts. This makes it a fruticose lichen.
107692.m: Reindeer lichen grows like a small shrub.

107693.e: Reindeer lichen is light grey to silvery. In large carpets, it can make the ground look almost white.
107693.m: Reindeer lichen is pale and silvery.

107694.q: About how fast does reindeer lichen grow?
a: Only a few millimetres a year
107694.e: Reindeer lichen grows only a few millimetres each year. A thick carpet of lichen is therefore often many decades old.

107695.q: How long does it take for a heavily grazed carpet of reindeer lichen to recover?
107695.e: Because the lichen grows so slowly, a grazed carpet needs decades to recover. That is why reindeer herds keep moving on.
107695.m: Grazed lichen carpets need decades to recover.

107696.q: Why was reindeer meat in Lapland contaminated after the Chernobyl nuclear accident in 1986?
a: The lichens stored radioactive caesium from the air
The reindeer ate fish from the Baltic Sea
The animals were given artificial feed
107696.e: Lichens take in substances directly from rain and air and store them for a long time. The reindeer ate the contaminated lichens, so the caesium got into their meat.
107696.m: Lichens store pollutants from the air for a very long time.

107697.q: What are reindeer lichens often used for in model making?
a: As bushes and little trees in model landscapes
107697.e: When dried, the branched lichens look like little bushes. Dyed, they are used in model railway landscapes and as decoration.
107697.m: Dried reindeer lichens are used as bushes in model making.

107698.q: Which two living things make up reindeer lichen?
107698.e: Every lichen is a partnership. The fungus gives support and stores water, and the alga makes nutrients using light.
107698.m: A lichen consists of a fungus and an alga.

107699.q: How does the royal fern reproduce?
107699.e: Like all ferns, the royal fern forms no flowers and no seeds. It reproduces with tiny spores.

107700.q: Where does the royal fern form its spores?
a: On brown leaflets at the tip of the fronds
In clusters on the underside of all leaflets
In capsules on long stalks on the ground
In cone-like spikes on separate shoots
107700.e: In the royal fern, the upper leaflets of some fronds have no leaf blade and are densely covered with sporangia. They look brown and branched like a flower head.
107700.m: In the royal fern, the spores sit at the tip of the fronds.

107701.q: Why is the royal fern also called the “flowering fern”?
a: Its spore clusters look like a flower head
It flowers every year in July
107701.e: Ferns never flower. But the brown spore clusters of the royal fern look so much like flowers that it got this nickname.
107701.m: The royal fern looks as if it is flowering, although ferns never flower.

107702.q: Because of its size, which ferns does the royal fern belong to?
a: The smallest ferns in the world
The tree ferns of the tropics
107702.e: The royal fern can grow well over a metre tall. It forms mighty clumps and is one of the largest ferns in Europe.
107702.m: The royal fern is one of the largest ferns in Europe.

107703.q: On which soils does the royal fern like to grow best?
a: On wet, acidic soils low in lime
On salty soils by the sea
107703.e: The royal fern needs a lot of water and soil low in lime. You find it in swampy woodland, by ditches and at the edges of bogs.
107703.m: The royal fern loves wet, acidic soils.

107704.q: What is special about the spores of the royal fern?
a: They contain chlorophyll and sprout very quickly
They are as big as peas
They can sprout for a hundred years
They can only sprout in salt water
107704.e: The spores of the royal fern are green because they contain chlorophyll. They must sprout quickly, because they only stay alive for a short time.
107704.m: Royal fern spores are green and short-lived.

107705.q: What do very old fossils of the royal fern family show?
a: These ferns have hardly changed for millions of years
Ferns used to have large flowers
Ferns used to live only in the sea
107705.e: Fossils about 180 million years old look very like today's royal ferns. Such plants are also called living fossils.
107705.m: Royal ferns have hardly changed for millions of years.

107706.q: How are the fronds of the royal fern divided?
107706.e: The fronds of the royal fern are twice divided. The individual leaflets are long and narrow and look like small leaves of broadleaved trees.
107706.m: The royal fern has twice-divided fronds.

107707.q: Which invention made Alfred Nobel rich before he wrote his will?
107707.e: Nobel invented dynamite in 1867 and earned a large fortune with it. In his will he decided that prizes should be paid for out of it.
107707.m: Alfred Nobel became rich with dynamite.

107708.q: Where does the money for the Nobel Prizes come from?
a: From the income on Nobel’s fortune
From taxes paid by the Swedish people
From entrance fees to the prize ceremony
107708.e: Nobel left almost his entire fortune to a foundation. The prizes are still paid for today out of the income from this money.
107708.m: Almost all of Nobel’s fortune went into the prizes.

107709.q: According to Nobel’s will, who should receive a prize?
a: Those who have brought the greatest benefit to humankind
Those who have donated the most money
Those who went to the best school in Sweden
Those who have registered the most patents
107709.e: The will says that the prizes should go to those who have done the greatest good for humankind. This idea still shapes the prizes today.
107709.m: The Nobel Prizes honour achievements that benefit humankind.

107710.q: According to Nobel’s will, what should play no part in choosing the prizewinners?
107710.e: Nobel wrote clearly that the candidates’ origin should not count. The most worthy person should receive the prize, no matter which country they come from.
107710.m: For the Nobel Prize, achievement counts, not origin.

107711.q: Which organisation was founded in 1900 to manage Nobel’s fortune?
107711.e: The Nobel Foundation manages the fortune and organises the prize ceremonies. However, it does not choose the prizewinners itself.
107711.m: The Nobel Foundation manages Alfred Nobel’s legacy.

107712.q: What does an executor of a will do, like the one Alfred Nobel had?
a: They make sure the last wishes are carried out
They write the will for the person who has died
107712.e: An executor carries out what is written in the will. For Nobel, this task was taken on by his young assistant Ragnar Sohlman.
107712.m: An executor carries out a person’s last wishes.

107713.q: Who fought against Nobel’s will after his death?
107713.e: Several relatives had hoped for a large inheritance and challenged the will. Only after an agreement could the first prizes be awarded in 1901.
107713.m: Nobel’s will was disputed at first.

107714.q: Which mistake by a newspaper in 1888 is said to have made Nobel think about his reputation?
a: It reported his death instead of his brother’s
It wrote that he had invented the telephone
It reported his marriage to a queen
107714.e: When his brother Ludvig died, an obituary of Alfred appeared that called him a merchant of death. This story is often told as the reason for the Nobel Prizes.
107714.m: A false obituary is said to have made Nobel think.

107715.q: In which city are most of the Nobel Prizes presented each year?
107715.e: Most Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm on 10 December, the day Nobel died. Only the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo.
107715.m: Most Nobel Prizes are awarded in Stockholm.

107716.q: Which famous physicist received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921?
107716.e: Einstein received the prize for explaining the photoelectric effect, not for the theory of relativity. Newton, Galileo and Archimedes lived long before there were Nobel Prizes.
107716.m: Albert Einstein received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1921.

107717.q: Who was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize, in 1903?
