107717.e: In 1903 Marie Curie, together with her husband Pierre and Henri Becquerel, received the Nobel Prize in Physics for research into radioactivity.
107717.m: Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

107718.q: Which particle, detected at CERN near Geneva in 2012, earned two physicists the Nobel Prize in 2013?
107718.e: Peter Higgs and François Englert had already predicted the particle in the 1960s. After it was detected at CERN, they received the Nobel Prize in 2013.
107718.m: The Higgs boson was detected at CERN in Switzerland.

107719.q: What did Rainer Weiss, Barry Barish and Kip Thorne receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 2017?
107719.e: Gravitational waves are tiny ripples in space-time that Einstein had predicted. They were measured for the first time in 2015 with huge measuring facilities.
107719.m: Gravitational waves were only measured directly in 2015.

107720.q: What was the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded for?
a: For extremely short flashes of light lasting attoseconds
107720.e: Pierre Agostini, Ferenc Krausz and Anne L’Huillier produced flashes of light lasting just a few attoseconds. With them, you can watch electrons move.
107720.m: With attosecond flashes of light, you can observe electrons.

107721.q: What did John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton receive the Nobel Prize in Physics for in 2024?
a: For the foundations of machine learning with artificial neural networks
107721.e: The two developed methods that allow artificial neural networks to learn. Today these are a foundation of artificial intelligence.
107721.m: The foundations of artificial intelligence were honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2024.

107722.q: How many women had received the Nobel Prize in Physics by 2026?
107722.e: After Marie Curie, Maria Goeppert Mayer, Donna Strickland, Andrea Ghez and Anne L’Huillier received the prize. That makes five women in total (as of 2026).
107722.m: Only a few women have received the Nobel Prize in Physics so far.

107723.q: What was the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics awarded to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for?
a: For quantum effects in electrical circuits
For measuring the speed of light
107723.e: The three showed that even a circuit you can hold in your hand can show quantum effects such as tunnelling. This is a foundation for quantum computers.
107723.m: Quantum effects also exist in larger electrical circuits.

107724.q: Which physicist received the Nobel Prize in 1918 for discovering energy quanta?
107724.e: In 1900 Max Planck realised that energy is only given off in small portions, called quanta. With this he founded quantum physics.
107724.m: Max Planck is seen as the founder of quantum physics.

107725.q: For which discovery did Marie Curie receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911?
a: For the elements radium and polonium
107725.e: Marie Curie discovered the radioactive elements radium and polonium. She named polonium after her home country, Poland.
107725.m: Marie Curie discovered radium and polonium.

107726.q: Can a person receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice?
a: Only if they come from Sweden
107726.e: Frederick Sanger received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1958 and 1980, and Barry Sharpless in 2001 and 2022. So both were honoured twice in the same subject.
107726.m: Some scientists have received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry twice.

107727.q: For which tool did Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020?
107727.e: With the CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors, genetic material can be changed very precisely. It was the first time that two women alone shared a Nobel Prize in science.
107727.m: The CRISPR/Cas9 gene scissors won the Nobel Prize in 2020.

107728.q: For which invention, found in almost every mobile phone today, was the Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded in 2019?
107728.e: John Goodenough, Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino developed the lithium-ion battery. It stores a lot of energy in a small space.
107728.m: The lithium-ion battery was honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2019.

107729.q: How old was John Goodenough when he received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019?
107729.e: John Goodenough was 97 years old. That makes him the oldest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize (as of 2026).
107729.m: The oldest Nobel prizewinner was 97 years old.

107730.q: What is Ernest Rutherford, who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1908, still famous for today?
a: For his model of the atom with a small nucleus
107730.e: Rutherford showed that almost all the mass of an atom is in a tiny nucleus. He received the Nobel Prize for his research into radioactivity.

107731.q: What is the ammonia from Fritz Haber’s process (Nobel Prize 1918) mainly used for?
107731.e: With the Haber-Bosch process, ammonia is made from nitrogen in the air. It is used to make artificial fertiliser, which today feeds a large part of humankind.
107731.m: The Haber-Bosch process provides ammonia for fertiliser.

107732.q: What was the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded for, partly to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper?
a: For predicting protein structures with artificial intelligence
107732.e: Their program AlphaFold can calculate the three-dimensional shape of proteins from their building blocks. The third prizewinner, David Baker, designed completely new proteins.
107732.m: Artificial intelligence can predict the shape of proteins.

107733.q: Which materials were honoured with the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2025?
107733.e: Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson and Omar Yaghi developed materials with tiny pores. These can, for example, store gases or collect water from desert air.
107733.m: Materials with tiny cavities can store gases.

107734.q: In which country is the decision on the Nobel Prize in Medicine made?
107734.e: The Nobel Prize in Medicine is voted on by 50 professors at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm.
107734.m: The Nobel Prize in Medicine is decided in Sweden.

107735.q: What did Emil von Behring receive the first Nobel Prize in Medicine for in 1901?
a: For a cure for a dangerous childhood disease
For the first pair of glasses
107735.e: Emil von Behring developed a healing serum against diphtheria. It saved the lives of many children.
107735.m: The first Nobel Prize in Medicine went to a cure for diphtheria.

107736.q: The Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1923 was for discovering which hormone?
107736.e: Frederick Banting and John Macleod were honoured for discovering insulin. Since then, people with diabetes can be treated.
107736.m: The discovery of insulin still saves many lives today.

107737.q: For which discovery did Watson, Crick and Wilkins receive the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1962?
a: For the double helix structure of DNA
107737.e: They showed that DNA is built like a twisted rope ladder. Important X-ray images for this had been made by Rosalind Franklin, who died in 1958.
107737.m: DNA has the shape of a double helix.

107738.q: Against which disease did Tu Youyou find a medicine, for which she received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2015?
107738.e: The Chinese scientist Tu Youyou discovered the drug artemisinin from a plant. It has saved the lives of millions of people with malaria.
107738.m: Artemisinin from a plant helps against malaria.

107739.q: For which research did Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman receive the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023?
a: For the foundations of mRNA vaccines
107739.e: Their research made it possible to use mRNA as a vaccine. This was crucial for the rapid development of Covid-19 vaccines.
107739.m: mRNA vaccines are based on the research of Karikó and Weissman.

107740.q: What did Alexander Fleming, who received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1945, discover?
107740.e: In 1928 Fleming discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic. He shared the Nobel Prize with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, who turned it into a medicine.

107741.q: What was the 2025 Nobel Prize in Medicine awarded for?
a: For discoveries about how the immune system spares the body’s own tissue
For a new medicine against headaches
107741.e: Mary Brunkow, Fred Ramsdell and Shimon Sakaguchi studied regulatory T cells. These stop the immune system from attacking the body itself.
107741.m: Regulatory T cells protect the body from its own immune system.

107742.q: Why is the Nobel Peace Prize awarded in Norway and not in Sweden?
a: In his will, Nobel chose a committee of the Norwegian parliament for it
Norway bought the right from Sweden
Alfred Nobel was born in Oslo
107742.e: In Nobel’s time, Sweden and Norway were joined in a union. Nobel decided that the Norwegian parliament should choose the jury for the Peace Prize.
107742.m: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded by a Norwegian committee.

107743.q: In which building is the Nobel Peace Prize presented today?
a: In the royal palace in Copenhagen
In the UN building in Geneva
107743.e: Since 1990 the ceremony has taken place in Oslo City Hall. The King and Queen of Norway are also present.
107743.m: The Nobel Peace Prize is presented in Oslo City Hall.

107744.q: Who, at 17, is the youngest person ever to receive a Nobel Prize?
107744.e: Malala Yousafzai campaigns for girls’ right to education. She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014.
107744.m: Malala is the youngest Nobel prizewinner.

107745.q: Which US civil rights campaigner received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 for his non-violent struggle against racial segregation?
107745.e: Martin Luther King campaigned without violence for equal rights for Black and white people. At 35, he was then the youngest winner of the Nobel Peace Prize.
107745.m: Martin Luther King fought non-violently for equal rights.

107746.q: Which two politicians jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993 for ending apartheid in South Africa?
a: Nelson Mandela and Frederik de Klerk
Jimmy Carter and Frederik de Klerk
107746.e: Mandela had been in prison for almost 30 years, and de Klerk was president. Together they led South Africa peacefully to elections for everyone.
107746.m: Mandela and de Klerk ended apartheid together.

107747.q: The German Carl von Ossietzky received the Nobel Peace Prize while he was held in a concentration camp. What did the Nazi government ban afterwards?
107747.e: Ossietzky had warned against Germany rearming. The government was furious about the honour and banned all Germans from accepting a Nobel Prize.
107747.m: Carl von Ossietzky was honoured with the Nobel Peace Prize while a prisoner.

107748.q: Which Japanese organisation received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2024?
a: Nihon Hidankyo, an association of atomic bomb survivors
107748.e: Nihon Hidankyo brings together survivors of the atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. They campaign for a world without nuclear weapons.
107748.m: Survivors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2024.

107749.q: What did María Corina Machado receive the Nobel Peace Prize for in 2025?
a: For her work for democracy in Venezuela
107749.e: The committee honoured the opposition politician for her work for democratic rights in Venezuela.
107749.m: The 2025 Nobel Peace Prize went to Venezuela.

107750.q: Why are the Nobel Prizes awarded every year on 10 December?
a: It is the day Alfred Nobel died
It is the shortest day of the year
107750.e: Alfred Nobel died on 10 December 1896. In memory of this, the ceremonies in Stockholm and Oslo take place on that day.
107750.m: The Nobel Prizes are presented on the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

107751.q: In which city does the big Nobel Banquet take place?
107751.e: The banquet takes place in the Blue Hall of Stockholm City Hall. Afterwards there is dancing in the Golden Hall.
107751.m: The Nobel Banquet takes place in Stockholm.

107752.q: Who, among others, attends the Nobel Banquet in Stockholm?
107752.e: Around 1,300 guests celebrate at the banquet, including the royal family and the prizewinners. The menu stays secret until the evening.
107752.m: The royal family celebrates at the Nobel Banquet.

107753.q: What did Alfred Nobel, whose fortune pays for the Nobel Prizes, invent?
107753.e: Alfred Nobel became rich with the explosive dynamite. In his will he decided that his fortune should be used for the Nobel Prizes.

107754.q: Which prize is awarded along with the Nobel Prizes but is not in Nobel’s will?
107754.e: In 1968 the Swedish Riksbank set up a prize in economic sciences in memory of Nobel. It has been awarded since 1969, but it is not a Nobel Prize in the sense of the will.
107754.m: The economics prize was only set up later by the Swedish Riksbank.

107755.q: Are you allowed to turn down a Nobel Prize?
a: Only for the Nobel Peace Prize
107755.e: In 1964 the French writer Jean-Paul Sartre turned down the Nobel Prize in Literature because he did not want any official honours. He is still counted as a prizewinner.
107755.m: You can turn down a Nobel Prize.

107756.q: What is the Nobel Prize in Literature awarded for?
a: For the work of a writer
For the best children’s book of the year
107756.e: Every year the Swedish Academy honours one person for their whole body of literary work. In 2025 the prize went to the Hungarian László Krasznahorkai.
107756.m: The Nobel Prize in Literature honours the work of a writer.

107757.q: What metal is a Nobel medal made of?
107757.e: Nobel medals are made of gold. Since 1980, 18-carat recycled gold has been used.
107757.m: The Nobel medal is made of gold.

107758.q: Whose face can be seen on the front of the Nobel medals?
107758.e: On the front, the medals show a portrait of Alfred Nobel, who founded the prizes.
107758.m: The Nobel medal shows Alfred Nobel.

107759.q: In which city is the Nobel Peace Prize presented with its medal?
107759.e: All the other Nobel Prizes are presented in Stockholm. Only the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo in Norway, as Alfred Nobel had decided.
107759.m: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo.

107760.q: What do Nobel prizewinners receive besides the medal?
107760.e: A Nobel Prize includes a gold medal, an artistically designed diploma and prize money of several million Swedish kronor.
107760.m: A Nobel Prize includes a medal, a diploma and prize money.

107761.q: In which language is the inscription on several Nobel medals written?
107761.e: The inscription “Inventas vitam iuvat excoluisse per artes” is Latin and comes from the Roman poet Virgil. Roughly, it means that inventions make life more beautiful.
107761.m: Nobel medals carry a Latin inscription.

107762.q: How did a chemist hide two gold Nobel medals from the German occupiers in Copenhagen in 1940?
a: He buried them in the garden
He melted them down into rings
107762.e: The chemist George de Hevesy dissolved the gold medals in a strong acid and put the bottle on a shelf. After the war the gold was recovered and the medals were cast again.
107762.m: Two Nobel medals survived the war dissolved in acid.

107763.q: Why did the journalist Dmitry Muratov sell his Nobel Peace Prize medal for over 100 million dollars in 2022?
a: To pay for a research ship
107763.e: The proceeds of over 100 million dollars went to the children’s charity UNICEF for refugee children from Ukraine. It was the highest price ever paid for a Nobel medal.
107763.m: The most expensive Nobel medal was sold for children in need.

107764.q: What is the Ig Nobel Prize awarded for?
a: For research that first makes people laugh and then makes them think
For the worst invention of the year
107764.e: The Ig Nobel Prize honours real but unusual research. The name is a play on the English word “ignoble”, meaning unworthy.
107764.m: The Ig Nobel Prize honours research that makes people laugh and think.

107765.q: Roughly how long has the Ig Nobel Prize existed?
107765.e: The Ig Nobel Prize was first awarded in 1991. Since then the ceremony has taken place every autumn.
107765.m: The Ig Nobel Prize has existed for over 30 years.

107766.q: Is the research that receives an Ig Nobel Prize real?
a: Yes, it is real but unusual research
No, it is completely made up
No, it is just jokes by comedians
107766.e: Real studies that sound strange or funny are honoured. Often there is still a serious question behind them.
107766.m: The Ig Nobel Prize honours real but unusual research.

107767.q: Who traditionally hands out the prizes at the Ig Nobel ceremony?
107767.e: At the ceremony, real Nobel prizewinners present the awards. This makes the event especially popular.
107767.m: Real Nobel prizewinners hand out the Ig Nobel Prizes.

107768.q: A scientist made an animal float using very strong magnets and received the Ig Nobel Prize for it. Which animal?
107768.e: In 2000 Andre Geim made a small frog float in a magnetic field. Ten years later he even received the real Nobel Prize in Physics.
107768.m: A floating frog won an Ig Nobel Prize.

107769.q: What prize money do the winners of the Ig Nobel Prize receive?
a: A banknote for 10 trillion Zimbabwe dollars
Nothing at all, not even a certificate
107769.e: The winners receive an invalid banknote from Zimbabwe with a value of 10 trillion dollars. It is practically worthless because inflation destroyed the value of the money there.
107769.m: The Ig Nobel prize money is practically worthless.

107770.q: What happens at the Ig Nobel ceremony if an acceptance speech goes on too long?
a: A child interrupts until the speech ends
The audience has to leave the hall
The speech is postponed until tomorrow
107770.e: The speeches have to be very short. Anyone who goes on too long is interrupted again and again by a girl saying “Please stop, I’m bored”.
107770.m: At the Ig Nobel ceremony, speeches must be short.

107771.q: What does the audience traditionally throw onto the stage at the Ig Nobel ceremony?
107771.e: The audience folds paper aeroplanes and throws them onto the stage during the ceremony. This custom has been a firm part of the event for years.
107771.m: Paper aeroplanes fly at the Ig Nobel ceremony.

107772.q: What does the Ig Nobel Prize want to spark in people?
107772.e: The research is meant first to make people laugh and then to make them think. In this way, more people should come to enjoy science.
107772.m: The Ig Nobel Prize makes people curious about science.

107773.q: Which Swiss man received the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901, together with Frédéric Passy?
107773.e: Henry Dunant from Geneva founded the Red Cross. He shared the first Nobel Peace Prize with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy.
107773.m: Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize.

107774.q: Which organisation based in Geneva has received the Nobel Peace Prize three times?
a: The International Committee of the Red Cross
107774.e: The International Committee of the Red Cross was honoured in 1917, 1944 and 1963. That gives it the record among Peace Prize winners.
107774.m: The ICRC has received the Nobel Peace Prize three times.

107775.q: In which field did the Swiss writer Carl Spitteler receive the Nobel Prize in 1919?
107775.e: Carl Spitteler from Liestal was honoured above all for his epic poem “Olympian Spring”. He is the only Nobel Prize winner in Literature born in Switzerland.
107775.m: Carl Spitteler received the Nobel Prize in Literature.

107776.q: What did the physicist Charles-Édouard Guillaume from Neuchâtel receive the Nobel Prize for in 1920?
a: For the metal alloy Invar, which hardly expands
For building the first cable car
107776.e: Invar hardly expands at all when it is warm. This was very important for precise measuring instruments and clocks.
107776.m: Invar is an alloy that hardly expands.

107777.q: Against which animals does DDT work, for which the Basel chemist Paul Müller received the Nobel Prize in 1948?
107777.e: Paul Müller discovered that DDT kills insects such as malaria mosquitoes. Later DDT was banned in many countries because of the harm it does to the environment.
107777.m: DDT was first celebrated and later banned because of environmental damage.

107778.q: Heinrich Rohrer and Gerd Binnig built a special microscope near Zurich. What could be made visible with it for the first time?
107778.e: With the scanning tunnelling microscope from the IBM research laboratory in Rüschlikon, individual atoms on surfaces could be seen for the first time. It won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986.
107778.m: The scanning tunnelling microscope makes individual atoms visible.

107779.q: For which discovery did Marie Curie receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911?
107779.e: Marie Curie and her husband discovered two new elements. She also managed to obtain pure radium.
107779.m: Marie Curie discovered two new chemical elements.

107780.q: What did Marie Curie become at the Sorbonne in Paris in 1906, as the first woman to do so?
107780.e: After her husband’s death, she took over his chair. This made her the first woman professor at the Sorbonne.
107780.m: Marie Curie was the first woman professor at the Sorbonne.

107781.q: Why are Marie Curie’s notebooks still kept in lead boxes today?
107781.e: Marie Curie worked with radioactive substances without protection. That is why her notebooks still give off radiation today and may only be looked at in protective clothing.
107781.m: Marie Curie’s notebooks still give off radiation today.

107782.q: Which chemical element was named after Marie and Pierre Curie?
107782.e: The artificial element curium has the atomic number 96. It was produced in 1944 and named in honour of the Curies.
107782.m: The element curium honours Marie and Pierre Curie.

107784.q: What, explicitly, did Einstein not receive the Nobel Prize for?
107784.e: The Nobel committee honoured him for his services to theoretical physics and for the photoelectric effect. The theory of relativity was deliberately not mentioned.
107784.m: Einstein did not get the Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity.

107785.q: What did the Danish physicist Niels Bohr study, who received a Nobel Prize at the same time as Einstein?
107785.e: Niels Bohr was honoured for his research into the structure of atoms. His prize and Einstein’s were announced together in November 1922.
107785.m: Niels Bohr studied the structure of atoms.

107786.q: What did Einstein talk about in his Nobel lecture in Gothenburg in 1923?
107786.e: Even though he did not get the prize for it, Einstein gave his talk on the theory of relativity. The audience was especially interested in it.
107786.m: Einstein spoke about the theory of relativity in his Nobel lecture.

107787.q: Why was the 1921 Physics Prize not awarded at first?
a: The committee found no candidate who met the rules
There was a war in Sweden
The foundation’s money had run out
Einstein had turned the prize down
107787.e: If no candidate is convincing, a prize may be postponed by one year. At that time many experts still had doubts about Einstein’s theories.
107787.m: A Nobel Prize can be postponed by one year.

107788.q: In which country is the Nobel Prize in Literature awarded?
107788.e: The Nobel Prize in Literature is awarded in Stockholm. Only the Nobel Peace Prize is awarded in Oslo in Norway.
107788.m: The Nobel Prize in Literature is awarded in Sweden.

107789.q: Who decides who gets the Nobel Peace Prize?
107789.e: The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded by a committee of five people who are elected by the Norwegian parliament. The other Nobel Prizes are decided in Sweden.
107789.m: A committee in Norway decides on the Nobel Peace Prize.

107790.q: How long do nominations for a Nobel Prize stay secret?
107790.e: The names of the nominees and the documents are only published after 50 years. This lets experts make suggestions freely and without pressure.
107790.m: Nobel Prize nominations stay secret for 50 years.

107791.q: Are you allowed to nominate yourself for a Nobel Prize?
a: Yes, but only once in your life
107791.e: Only selected people may make nominations, for example professors, members of academies or former prizewinners. Anyone who nominates themselves is not considered.
107791.m: For a Nobel Prize, you have to be nominated by others.

107792.q: In which month are the Nobel prizewinners announced each year?
107792.e: The committees examine the nominations from February until the autumn. The prizewinners are announced in October and receive the prize in December.
107792.m: The Nobel prizewinners are announced in October.

107793.q: Can you get a Nobel Prize if you have already died?
a: No, only living people are newly honoured
Yes, that is actually the rule
Yes, but only the Nobel Peace Prize
Only if the family applies for it
107793.e: Since 1974 only living people may be honoured. One exception was Ralph Steinman in 2011: he died shortly before the announcement without the committee knowing, and he kept the prize.
107793.m: The Nobel Prize is only awarded to living people.

107794.q: For which of these subjects is there a Nobel Prize?
107794.e: Alfred Nobel set up prizes for physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace. There is no Nobel Prize for mathematics.
107794.m: Chemistry is one of the subjects with a Nobel Prize.

107795.q: Can an organisation also receive the Nobel Peace Prize?
a: Yes, for example the Red Cross
Only companies with lots of money
107795.e: The International Committee of the Red Cross from Geneva even received the Nobel Peace Prize three times: in 1917, 1944 and 1963.
107795.m: Organisations such as the Red Cross can also receive the Nobel Peace Prize.

107796.q: What was the work about for which Einstein later received the Nobel Prize?
107796.e: In 1905 Einstein published a paper about light and the photoelectric effect. Many years passed before he was honoured for it.
107796.m: Einstein’s Nobel Prize work was about light.

107797.q: What was the first part of the official reason given for Einstein’s Nobel Prize?
a: For his services to theoretical physics
For his work as a teacher
107797.e: The committee honoured him for his services to theoretical physics and especially for the law of the photoelectric effect. The theory of relativity was deliberately not mentioned.
107797.m: Einstein was honoured for his services to theoretical physics.

107798.q: Why was Einstein’s theory of relativity not mentioned for his Nobel Prize?
a: Some experts did not yet think it had been proved
It had not yet been published
107798.e: Some members of the Nobel committee, such as Allvar Gullstrand, had doubts about the theory of relativity. So Einstein was honoured for other work.
107798.m: Einstein’s theory of relativity was disputed in the Nobel committee.

107799.q: In 1905, what did Einstein call the small portions of energy that light is made of?
107799.e: Einstein explained that light carries energy in small packets. Today these light quanta are called photons.
107799.m: Light is made of small portions of energy.

107800.q: From which ore did Marie Curie obtain radium through painstaking work?
107800.e: Marie Curie processed tonnes of pitchblende, an ore containing uranium. In the end she obtained only tiny amounts of the new element.

107801.q: What is measured with the old unit called the “curie”?
107801.e: The curie was originally based on the radiation from one gram of radium. Today radioactivity is usually measured in becquerels.
107801.m: An old unit of radioactivity is called the curie.

107802.q: How did Pierre Curie die in 1906?
a: He was run over by a horse-drawn cart in Paris
He died in a laboratory fire
107802.e: Pierre Curie slipped on a wet street in the rain and fell under a heavy horse-drawn cart. Marie Curie carried on their joint research alone.
107802.m: After Pierre’s death, Marie Curie carried on her research alone.

107803.q: The Basel scientist Tadeus Reichstein received the Nobel Prize in 1950 for his research on cortisone. What is cortisone?
107803.e: Cortisone is a hormone from the adrenal cortex. It is still used today as a medicine against inflammation.
107803.m: Tadeus Reichstein studied the hormone cortisone.

107804.q: Rolf Zinkernagel received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1996. Which system of the body did he study?
107804.e: Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty showed how immune cells recognise body cells infected by viruses. This is important for understanding vaccinations.
107804.m: Rolf Zinkernagel studied the immune system.

107805.q: Karl Alexander Müller received the Nobel Prize in 1987 for his research on superconductors. What can superconductors do?
107805.e: Superconductors conduct electric current without any loss. At the IBM laboratory in Rüschlikon, Müller and Georg Bednorz discovered substances that can do this at comparatively high temperatures.

107806.q: Who gives the short thank-you speeches at the Nobel Banquet in Stockholm?
a: One person from each prize category
107806.e: At the end of the banquet, one prizewinner per prize category steps up to the lectern. The speeches last only a few minutes.
107806.m: At the Nobel Banquet, the prizewinners give short speeches.

107807.q: What are the two large branches called into which the windpipe divides at the bottom?
107807.e: The windpipe splits into a right and a left main bronchus. Each leads to one lung.
107807.m: The windpipe divides into two main bronchi.

107809.q: What supports the walls of the larger bronchi so they stay open when you breathe?
107809.e: In the walls of the larger bronchi there are rings and plates of cartilage. They stop the tubes from collapsing.
107809.m: Cartilage keeps the large bronchi open.

107810.q: What is an inflammation of the bronchi called?
107810.e: The ending “-itis” means inflammation. Bronchitis affects the lining of the bronchi and often causes a cough with mucus.
107810.m: In bronchitis, the bronchi are inflamed.

107811.q: What is the examination called in which a doctor looks into the bronchi with a thin tube with a camera?
107811.e: In a bronchoscopy, an endoscope is pushed through the nose or mouth and the windpipe into the bronchi. This lets doctors look at the airways from the inside.
107811.m: A bronchoscopy looks inside the bronchi.

107812.q: Where do the two main bronchi lead?
107812.e: The windpipe divides into a right and a left main bronchus. Each one carries air into one lung.
107812.m: Each main bronchus leads to one lung.

107813.q: What is the mucus in the bronchi for?
a: Dust and germs stick to it
107813.e: The mucus traps dust and germs. Tiny hair-like cilia then move it up to the throat.

107814.q: Why do many long-term smokers cough in the morning?
a: Smoke damages the cilia and mucus builds up
Smoke only dries out the mouth
Smoke cools the lungs too much
107814.e: Tobacco smoke paralyses and destroys the cilia. The mucus is no longer carried away and has to be coughed up.
107814.m: Tobacco smoke damages the self-cleaning of the bronchi.

107815.q: Why are the bronchi also called the bronchial tree?
107815.e: The windpipe divides into two main bronchi, and these divide again and again into smaller branches. It looks like an upside-down tree.
107815.m: The bronchi branch like a tree.

107816.q: What are the finest branches of the bronchi called, just before the air sacs begin?
107816.e: After many branchings, the bronchi become bronchioles. They carry the air all the way to the air sacs.
107816.m: The bronchioles are the finest branches of the bronchial tree.

107817.q: How do the airways change the deeper they go into the lungs?
107817.e: With each branching, the tubes become narrower. The finest bronchioles are thinner than a millimetre.
107817.m: The deeper in the lungs, the thinner the airways.

107818.q: Roughly how wide is a bronchiole?
107818.e: Bronchioles are the airways with a diameter of less than about one millimetre. So they are thinner than a pencil lead.
107818.m: Bronchioles are thinner than a millimetre.

107819.q: What can the smooth muscles in the walls of the bronchioles do?
a: Make the airways narrower or wider
107819.e: When the smooth muscles contract, the bronchioles get narrower. When they relax, air flows more easily.
107819.m: Smooth muscles control how wide the bronchioles are.

107820.q: Where do the finest airways in the lungs end?
107820.e: At the end of the finest bronchioles sit millions of tiny air sacs. There the air you breathe comes very close to the blood.
107820.m: The airways end in the air sacs.

107821.q: What happens in the air sacs of the lungs?
a: Oxygen goes into the blood, carbon dioxide comes out
107821.e: The walls of the air sacs are wafer-thin and surrounded by fine blood vessels. So oxygen can pass into the blood and carbon dioxide into the air.
107821.m: Gas exchange takes place in the air sacs.

107822.q: What is an inflammation of the bronchioles called that mainly affects babies?
107822.e: In bronchiolitis, the fine bronchioles swell and get blocked with mucus. Babies, with their very narrow airways, are especially affected.
107822.m: Bronchiolitis is an inflammation of the finest airways.

107823.q: Why do babies become especially ill when their fine airways are inflamed?
a: They only breathe through their mouth
Their airways are made of cartilage
107823.e: Even a little swelling or some mucus can block a baby's tiny airways. That is why they get short of breath more easily.

107824.q: What is the “Adam's apple” on the neck?
107824.e: The Adam's apple is the front edge of one of the cartilages of the larynx. In men it is usually easy to see.
107824.m: The Adam's apple is part of the larynx.

107825.q: Between which parts of the airways is the larynx?
a: Between the throat and the windpipe
Between the nose and the throat
Between the windpipe and the bronchi
Between the bronchi and the lungs
107825.e: The larynx joins the throat at the top and leads into the windpipe. It forms the entrance to the lower airways.
107825.m: The larynx connects the throat with the windpipe.

107826.q: What in the larynx produces our voice?
107826.e: The vocal folds are in the larynx. When air flows through, they vibrate and make sounds.
107826.m: The voice is made by the vocal folds in the larynx.

107827.q: What is a typical sign of laryngitis?
107827.e: In laryngitis, the vocal folds are also irritated and swollen. That is why the voice becomes hoarse.

107828.q: What is especially typical of croup in young children?
107828.e: In croup, the lining of the larynx below the vocal folds swells, usually because of a virus. A barking cough and noisy breathing, often at night, are typical.
107828.m: You can recognise croup by its barking cough.

107829.q: What do the vocal folds do when we speak?
a: They pull back into the ear
107829.e: When we speak, the vocal folds are brought together. The air we breathe out makes them vibrate, and this creates a sound.
107829.m: Vibrating vocal folds produce the voice.

107830.q: Why do boys' voices get deeper when their voices break?
a: The larynx and vocal folds grow
107830.e: During puberty the larynx grows and the vocal folds get longer. Longer vocal folds vibrate more slowly, so the voice sounds deeper.
107830.m: Longer vocal folds give a deeper voice.

107831.q: What can babies do thanks to their high larynx that adults cannot?
a: Drink and breathe at the same time
107831.e: In babies, the larynx sits high up. Milk can flow past the sides of the entrance to the larynx while air flows through the nose.
107831.m: Babies can drink and breathe at the same time.

107832.q: What job does the epiglottis do?
a: It closes off the windpipe when you swallow
It warms the air you breathe
107832.e: When you swallow, the epiglottis folds over the larynx. This way food goes into the oesophagus and not into the windpipe.
107832.m: The epiglottis protects the windpipe when you swallow.

107833.q: What forms the framework of the epiglottis?
107833.e: The epiglottis contains elastic cartilage. That is why it is flexible and springs back into place after swallowing.
107833.m: The epiglottis is made of flexible, elastic cartilage.

a: Behind the root of the tongue
At the end of the windpipe
107834.e: The epiglottis rises behind the root of the tongue above the entrance to the larynx. From there it can cover the larynx.
107834.m: The epiglottis sits behind the root of the tongue.

107835.q: Which reflex pushes food back out if it slips past the epiglottis into the larynx?
107835.e: If something gets into the larynx, the sensitive lining immediately triggers a cough. The strong blast of air throws the object out.
107835.m: Coughing protects the airways from foreign objects.

107836.q: Why is severe swelling of the epiglottis dangerous?
107836.e: If the epiglottis swells badly during an infection, it can block the way to the windpipe. This is an emergency.
107836.m: Inflammation of the epiglottis is a medical emergency.

107837.q: What protects children well from epiglottitis today?
107837.e: The most common cause was a bacterium that babies are now vaccinated against. Since then the disease has become rare in children.

107838.q: Why should you not laugh or talk with your mouth full?
a: The larynx is open while you do it
The oesophagus is closed while you do it
The stomach closes while you do it
The teeth get in the way
107838.e: When you speak and laugh, air flows through the open larynx. The epiglottis cannot cover it safely then, and food can easily go down the wrong way.
107838.m: The larynx stays open when you speak.

107839.q: What is the gap between the two vocal folds called?
107839.e: The vocal folds form the left and right edges of the glottis. The air you breathe flows through it.
107839.m: The glottis lies between the vocal folds.

107840.q: During which part of breathing do we normally produce our voice?
107840.e: The air flowing out makes the almost closed vocal folds vibrate. This creates the sound.

107841.q: How does the voice get higher?
a: The vocal folds are stretched more tightly
107841.e: Tight vocal folds vibrate faster. More vibrations per second give a higher note.
107841.m: The tighter the vocal folds, the higher the voice.

107842.q: Why do men usually have a deeper voice than women?
a: Their vocal folds are longer and thicker
107842.e: Longer and thicker vocal folds vibrate more slowly. That is why the voice sounds deeper, much like a thick guitar string.
107842.m: Longer vocal folds produce deeper notes.

107843.q: What is a common cause of “singer's nodules” on the vocal folds?
a: Too little sleep at the weekend
107843.e: If you often use your voice too loudly or in the wrong way, you irritate the vocal folds. Small thickenings can form there and make you hoarse.

107844.q: Where in the body are the vocal folds?
a: In the back of the nose
107844.e: The vocal folds are stretched inside the larynx between its cartilages. That is why the larynx is also called the voice box.
107844.m: The vocal folds are in the larynx.

107845.q: How many times per second do the vocal folds vibrate when someone sings a note of 220 hertz?
107845.e: One hertz means one vibration per second. At 220 hertz, the vocal folds therefore vibrate 220 times per second.
107845.m: The pitch matches the number of vibrations per second.

107846.q: How are the vocal folds positioned during quiet breathing?
107846.e: When you breathe, the glottis is wide open so that air can flow freely. Only for speaking are the vocal folds brought close together.
107846.m: When you breathe, the glottis is wide open.

107847.q: By which process does oxygen pass from the air sacs into the blood?
107847.e: Particles move by themselves from a place of high concentration to a place of low concentration. There is more oxygen in the air sacs than in the blood arriving there.
107847.m: In gas exchange, the gases move by diffusion.

107848.q: Roughly how many air sacs does an adult have?
107848.e: The number of air sacs is estimated at around 300 million or more. This creates a huge surface in a small space.
107848.m: The lungs contain hundreds of millions of air sacs.

107849.q: Roughly how large is the surface of all the air sacs together?
107849.e: Spread out, all the air sacs would cover about 100 square metres. That is roughly the floor area of a large flat.
107849.m: The gas exchange surface of the lungs is as large as a flat.

107850.q: What are the finest blood vessels called that wrap around the air sacs like a net?
107850.e: Capillaries are the thinnest blood vessels. Their walls lie close against the walls of the air sacs so that gases can pass quickly.
107850.m: Capillaries wrap around the air sacs.

107851.q: At rest, roughly how long does a red blood cell stay in contact with an air sac?
107851.e: Blood flows quickly through the capillaries of the lungs; at rest the contact time is only about three quarters of a second. It is still enough, because the gases pass across very quickly.
107851.m: Gas exchange in the lungs takes less than a second.

107852.q: Why is the wall between the air sacs and the blood extremely thin?
a: So the gases can pass through quickly
So no germs can get in
107852.e: The dividing wall is thinner than a thousandth of a millimetre. The shorter the path, the faster the gases pass through.
107852.m: A thin wall speeds up gas exchange.

107853.q: Roughly how much oxygen does the air you breathe out contain?
107853.e: The lungs take only about a quarter of the oxygen from the air. So the air you breathe out still contains about 16 per cent oxygen.
107853.m: Breathed-out air still contains about 16 per cent oxygen.

107854.q: Why is carbon monoxide so dangerous for gas exchange?
a: It takes oxygen's place on haemoglobin
It clogs the bronchi with soot
It destroys the ribs at once
It makes the air too damp
107854.e: Carbon monoxide binds much more strongly to the red blood pigment than oxygen does. The blood can then hardly carry any oxygen.
107854.m: Carbon monoxide pushes oxygen out of the blood.

107856.q: Roughly how many breaths per minute does a healthy newborn baby take at rest?
107856.e: Newborn babies breathe much faster than adults, about 40 times per minute. The breathing rate drops with age.
107856.m: Babies breathe much faster than adults.

107857.q: Where is the respiratory centre that controls breathing?
107857.e: In the brainstem, in the medulla oblongata, there are nerve cells that set the rhythm of breathing. That is why we also breathe while asleep.
107857.m: The respiratory centre is in the brainstem.

107858.q: Which change in the blood stimulates breathing the most?
107858.e: Sensors measure the amount of carbon dioxide in the blood. If it rises, we breathe faster and deeper.
107858.m: A lot of carbon dioxide in the blood drives breathing.

107859.q: An adult breathes in 15 times a minute, 0.5 litres of air each time. How much air does he breathe in per minute?
107859.e: You multiply the number of breaths by the amount of air per breath: 15 times 0.5 litres makes 7.5 litres. This is called the minute volume.
107859.m: Minute volume is breathing rate times the volume of each breath.

107860.q: You count 9 breaths from a classmate in 30 seconds. What is her breathing rate per minute?
107860.e: A minute has 60 seconds, twice as long as 30 seconds. 9 times 2 makes 18 breaths per minute.
107860.m: The breathing rate gives the number of breaths per minute.

107861.q: What happens to your breathing rate when you run fast?
107861.e: When you run, your muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide. That is why you breathe faster.
107861.m: When you make an effort, you breathe faster.

a: They breathe out too much carbon dioxide
They no longer take in any oxygen
107862.e: Anyone who breathes too fast and too deeply, for example when upset, gives off too much carbon dioxide. Tingling in the hands and lips and dizziness are typical results.
107862.m: When hyperventilating, you breathe too fast and too deeply.

107863.q: Why do you breathe faster high in the mountains than in the lowlands?
107863.e: At altitude the air pressure is lower, so the air is thinner. With each breath less oxygen reaches the lungs, so you breathe faster.
107863.m: At altitude you have to breathe faster because the air is thinner.

107864.q: Which sound is typical when breathing out during an asthma attack?
107864.e: The narrowed airways only let the air out with difficulty. This creates a whistling or humming sound.
107864.m: Wheezing is a sign of asthma.

107865.q: What happens to the airways during an asthma attack?
107865.e: The muscles around the bronchi tighten, the lining swells and makes thick mucus. Air has trouble getting out.
107865.m: During an asthma attack, the bronchi become narrow.

107866.q: What can trigger an attack in allergic asthma?
107866.e: In allergic asthma, the immune system reacts to harmless substances such as pollen, house dust mites or animal hair. The airways become inflamed and narrow.
107866.m: Pollen can trigger asthma in people with allergies.

107867.q: What is a reliever inhaler for in asthma?
107867.e: The medicine relaxes the muscles around the bronchi within minutes. This lets you breathe better again quickly.
107867.m: A reliever inhaler opens the bronchi quickly.

107868.q: What does a peak flow meter measure?
a: How fast you can breathe out at most
How much sugar is in the blood
107868.e: You blow into the device as hard as you can. If the value drops, the airways are narrower than usual.
107868.m: A peak flow meter shows how clear the airways are.

107869.e: Asthma is a long-term inflammation of the airways, not an infection. You cannot catch it from someone.
107869.m: Asthma is not a contagious illness.

107870.q: What is an inhaler aid called a spacer for?
a: You no longer have to breathe in
107870.e: The spacer is a chamber between the inhaler and the mouth. The spray mist spreads out inside it and can be breathed in calmly instead of getting stuck in the mouth.
107870.m: With a spacer, the medicine gets into the lungs better.

107871.q: What is bronchial asthma, at its core?
a: A long-term inflammation of the airways
107871.e: In asthma, the airways are permanently inflamed and oversensitive. That is why they react to triggers by narrowing.
107871.m: Asthma is a lasting inflammation of the airways.

107872.q: Can a child with well-treated asthma do sport?
107872.e: With the right treatment, most children with asthma can do sport normally. For exercise-induced asthma, an inhaler before training and a good warm-up often help.

107873.q: What is the medical term for an infection of the lungs?
107873.e: “Pneumon” is Greek for lung. Pleurisy affects the lining of the chest, and a pneumothorax is air in the chest cavity.
107873.m: An infection of the lungs is called pneumonia.

107874.q: Which bacteria most often cause pneumonia outside hospital?
107874.e: Pneumococci are the most common bacterial cause of pneumonia caught outside hospital. Their name refers to the lungs.
107874.m: Pneumococci are common causes of pneumonia.

107875.q: Which sounds does a doctor often hear with a stethoscope in pneumonia?
107875.e: When the person breathes, fine crackling sounds can be heard over the inflamed part of the lung. They are called crackles.

107876.q: For whom is pneumonia especially dangerous?
107876.e: In older people and people with a weak immune system, pneumonia more often becomes serious. It can also be dangerous for very young children.
107876.m: Older people are especially at risk from pneumonia.

107877.q: Which examination is often used to confirm pneumonia?
107877.e: On an X-ray, inflamed areas of the lung show up as pale shadows. Listening to the chest and blood tests are added to this.

107878.q: Which symptoms are typical of pneumonia?
a: Fever, cough and shortness of breath
Toothache and ringing in the ears
107878.e: The inflammation in the lungs causes fever and a cough. Because fewer air sacs are working, shortness of breath often comes too.
107878.m: Fever, cough and shortness of breath point to pneumonia.

107879.q: Which vaccine protects against a common form of pneumonia?
107879.e: The pneumococcal vaccine protects against these bacteria. In Switzerland it is recommended for babies and older people.
107879.m: The pneumococcal vaccine helps prevent pneumonia.

107880.q: What collects in the affected air sacs in pneumonia?
107880.e: The inflamed air sacs fill with fluid and immune cells. Hardly any oxygen can then pass into the blood there.
107880.m: In pneumonia, air sacs are filled with fluid.

a: Breathing in other people's tobacco smoke
107881.e: Anyone who stays near people smoking breathes in their smoke too. The same harmful substances get into the lungs.
107881.m: Passive smoking means breathing in other people's tobacco smoke.

107882.q: Where in Switzerland is smoking generally banned to protect people from passive smoking?
107882.e: The federal law on protection against passive smoking has applied since 2010. Smoking is generally banned in enclosed spaces such as restaurants, schools and shops.
107882.m: Smoking is banned in enclosed public spaces.

107883.q: What is the smoke called that rises from the burning cigarette between puffs?
107883.e: Mainstream smoke is drawn in by the person smoking. Sidestream smoke rises freely into the room and is breathed in by everyone there.
107883.m: Sidestream smoke goes straight into the air of the room.

107884.q: Why is sidestream smoke considered especially harmful?
a: Many harmful substances in it are more concentrated
It is hotter than a fire
107884.e: Because the cigarette smoulders at a lower temperature between puffs, the tobacco burns less completely. So many toxins are more concentrated in sidestream smoke.
107884.m: Sidestream smoke is often more toxic than the smoke drawn in.

107885.q: Which airway disease is more common in children who often breathe in second-hand smoke?
107885.e: Tobacco smoke irritates children's sensitive airways. That is why they get asthma and bronchitis more often.
107885.m: Second-hand smoke increases the risk of asthma in children.

107886.q: Why is smoking in a car especially harmful for passengers?
a: The smoke builds up in the small space
The engine draws in the smoke
107886.e: In the cramped interior, harmful substances quickly reach very high concentrations. Even an open window makes little difference.
107886.m: In a car, smoke becomes especially concentrated.

107887.q: In Switzerland, what is a separate, ventilated smoking room in a restaurant called?
107887.e: Federal law generally bans smoking in the enclosed rooms of restaurants. Separate, well-ventilated smoking rooms called fumoirs are allowed.
107887.m: A fumoir is a separate smoking room.

107888.q: Does a window left slightly open protect children in a flat from tobacco smoke?
a: Yes, if it is cold outside
107888.e: Smoke spreads quickly into all rooms, and harmful substances settle in furniture and curtains. Only a smoke-free home gives real protection.
107888.m: Only a smoke-free home really protects children.

107889.q: What is meant by vital capacity?
a: The largest amount of air you can breathe out after breathing in deeply
The amount of air you breathe in and out in one quiet breath
The amount of air that always stays in the lungs after breathing out
The amount of air you breathe in during a whole day
107889.e: You breathe in as deeply as possible and then breathe out as completely as possible. The amount breathed out is the vital capacity.
107889.m: Vital capacity is the largest amount of air you can breathe in and out again.

107890.q: Which device is used at the doctor's to measure vital capacity?
107890.e: With a spirometer you blow into a mouthpiece. The device measures how much air flows and how fast.
107890.m: A spirometer measures the amounts of air in the lungs.

107891.q: Roughly how large is the vital capacity of a healthy adult?
107891.e: In adults, the vital capacity is usually between about 3 and 5 litres. It depends on things such as height, age and training.
107891.m: Adults have a vital capacity of a few litres.

107892.q: Are the lungs completely empty after breathing out as hard as you can?
a: No, about 1 to 1.5 litres of air stay in them
Yes, they are then completely empty
No, they are then still half full of water
107892.e: Even when you breathe out as far as possible, some air stays in the lungs. It stops the air sacs from collapsing.
107892.m: Some air always remains in the lungs.

107893.q: Tidal volume 0.5 litres, inspiratory reserve 3 litres, expiratory reserve 1 litre: what is the vital capacity?
107893.e: The vital capacity is the sum of the tidal volume and both reserve volumes. 0.5 plus 3 plus 1 makes 4.5 litres.
107893.m: Vital capacity is made up of the tidal volume and the two reserve volumes.

107894.q: A person has a vital capacity of 4.5 litres and a residual volume of 1.5 litres. How much air do their lungs hold in total?
107894.e: Total lung capacity is the vital capacity plus the residual air. 4.5 plus 1.5 makes 6 litres.
107894.m: Add the residual air to the vital capacity to get the total lung capacity.

107895.q: What does vital capacity depend on, among other things?
a: Whether you are left- or right-handed
107895.e: Taller people usually have a larger ribcage and larger lungs. Age, sex and training also play a part.
107895.m: Tall people usually have a larger vital capacity.

107896.q: How does vital capacity usually change in old age?
107896.e: With age, the lungs and ribcage become less elastic. That is why you can move less air.
107896.m: Vital capacity falls in old age.

107897.q: How can you easily estimate your own vital capacity at school?
a: Breathe out into an upside-down bottle filled with water
Count your pulse for one minute
Hold your breath and count the seconds
Measure your chest with a tape measure
107897.e: You breathe in deeply and blow through a tube into an upside-down bottle filled with water. The amount of water pushed out equals the air breathed out.
107897.m: Vital capacity can be measured by water displacement.

107898.q: Where in the body is the carbon dioxide made that we breathe out?
107898.e: In cellular respiration, nutrients are broken down using oxygen. This produces carbon dioxide, which travels in the blood to the lungs.
107898.m: Carbon dioxide is made in all cells during cellular respiration.

107899.q: How does carbon dioxide get from the cells to the lungs?
107899.e: Carbon dioxide from the cells is taken up by the blood and carried to the lungs. There we breathe it out.
107899.m: The blood carries carbon dioxide to the lungs.

107900.q: How can you detect carbon dioxide in a school experiment?
a: A glowing splint bursts into flame
107900.e: If you bubble carbon dioxide through limewater, insoluble chalk forms and the water turns milky. A glowing splint that relights, on the other hand, shows oxygen.

107901.q: What does a CO2 traffic light in a classroom show?
a: When the room should be aired
107901.e: As people breathe out, the carbon dioxide level in the room rises. If the light shows yellow or red, you should open the windows, because otherwise tiredness and concentration problems increase.
107901.m: A CO2 traffic light reminds you to air the room.

107902.q: Is carbon dioxide heavier or lighter than air?
107902.e: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air and collects near the floor, for example in fermentation cellars. There it can put people in danger.
107902.m: Carbon dioxide collects near the floor because it is heavier than air.

107903.q: How much of the outdoor air is carbon dioxide?
107903.e: Air is made up mainly of nitrogen and oxygen. Carbon dioxide makes up only about 0.04 per cent.
107903.m: Air contains only very little carbon dioxide.

107904.q: What do green plants do with the carbon dioxide we breathe out?
a: They use it to build sugar
107904.e: In photosynthesis, plants use light, water and carbon dioxide. From these, sugar and oxygen are made.
107904.m: Plants use carbon dioxide for photosynthesis.

107905.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a microphone?
107905.e: The sound waves make a thin diaphragm in the microphone vibrate. This movement is turned into electrical signals.
107905.m: A microphone turns sound into electrical signals.

107906.q: Which energy conversion mainly takes place in a hair dryer?
a: Electrical energy into heat and movement
107906.e: In a hair dryer, a heating wire heats the air and a small motor drives the fan. Both run on electrical energy.
107906.m: A hair dryer turns electrical energy into heat and movement.

107908.q: Which energy conversion happens in a bicycle dynamo?
107908.e: The turning wheel drives the dynamo, which produces electricity like a small generator. This makes the bicycle light shine.
107908.m: A dynamo produces electrical energy from movement.

107909.q: Why can no device turn 100 per cent of the energy it receives into useful energy?
a: Some of the energy is destroyed
107909.e: With every conversion, friction and other effects also produce heat, which usually cannot be used. The energy is not lost, but it is no longer useful.
107909.m: Every energy conversion also produces unused heat.

107910.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a glowing firefly?
107910.e: A chemical reaction takes place in the firefly’s light organ that produces light. This is called bioluminescence.
107910.m: Fireflies produce light from chemical energy.

107911.q: A motor receives 200 joules of electrical energy and gives out 150 joules of kinetic energy. What is its efficiency?
107911.e: Efficiency is useful energy divided by energy supplied: 150 J divided by 200 J gives 0.75. That is 75 per cent.
107911.m: Efficiency is always below 100 per cent.

107912.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a loudspeaker?
107912.e: The electric current moves a diaphragm in the loudspeaker back and forth. This makes the air vibrate, and we hear sound.
107912.m: A loudspeaker turns electrical energy into sound.

107913.q: What does the potential energy of an object on Earth depend on?
107913.e: The heavier an object is and the higher it is, the more potential energy it has. The strength of gravity also plays a part.
107913.m: Heavy objects high up have a lot of potential energy.

107914.q: Which formula is used to calculate potential energy?
107914.e: You multiply mass, acceleration due to gravity and height. On Earth, g is about 9.81 newtons per kilogram.
107914.m: Potential energy is the product of mass, acceleration due to gravity and height.

107915.q: A 2 kg stone lies 5 m above the ground. How much potential energy does it have relative to the ground (g = 10 N/kg)?
107915.e: You calculate m times g times h: 2 kg times 10 N/kg times 5 m gives 100 joules.
107915.m: Twice the mass or twice the height means twice the potential energy.

107916.q: A 60 kg hiker climbs 1000 metres up a mountain. How much potential energy does she gain (g = 10 N/kg)?
107916.e: 60 kg times 10 N/kg times 1000 m gives 600,000 joules. That is 600 kilojoules.
107916.m: When you climb a mountain, you gain a lot of potential energy.

107917.q: How does the potential energy change if you lift an object twice as high?
107917.e: In the formula, height is simply a factor. Twice the height therefore gives twice the potential energy.
107917.m: Potential energy grows in the same proportion as height.

107918.q: A 1 kg book is moved from a 0.8 m high table to a 2 m high shelf. How much potential energy does it gain (g = 10 N/kg)?
107918.e: The book is lifted by 2 m minus 0.8 m, which is 1.2 m. 1 kg times 10 N/kg times 1.2 m gives 12 joules.
107918.m: Only the difference in height counts for the potential energy gained.

107919.q: What does the Nant de Drance pumped-storage power station in Valais do when there is too much electricity in the grid?
a: It pumps water up into a higher reservoir
It lets water out into the valley
It switches off all its machines
107919.e: With surplus electricity, the power station pumps water upwards. Up there, the water has more potential energy, which can later be turned back into electricity.
107919.m: A pumped-storage power station stores electricity as the potential energy of water.

107920.q: A stone on the Moon is at the same height above the ground as on Earth. How does its potential energy compare?
a: Greater, because there is no air
Zero, because the Moon has no water
107920.e: The acceleration due to gravity on the Moon is only about one sixth of that on Earth. That is why the potential energy is smaller too.
107920.m: On the Moon, potential energy is smaller than on Earth.

107921.q: Why do you always have to choose a zero level for potential energy?
a: Height is measured from a chosen reference point
Because energy would otherwise be negative
107921.e: A book on a table has no potential energy relative to the table, but it does have some relative to the floor. So it depends on the chosen reference height.
107921.m: Potential energy always applies relative to a chosen zero level.

107922.q: Which formula is used to calculate kinetic energy?
107922.e: Kinetic energy depends on the mass and on the square of the speed. That is why v is squared.
107922.m: Kinetic energy is calculated from the mass and the speed squared.

107923.q: How does the kinetic energy change if the speed doubles?
a: It becomes eight times as great
107923.e: The speed is squared in the formula. 2 times 2 gives 4, so the energy becomes four times as great.
107923.m: Twice the speed means four times the kinetic energy.

107924.q: A 2 kg ball rolls at 3 m/s. How great is its kinetic energy?
107924.e: You calculate ½ times 2 kg times 3 m/s squared: 0.5 times 2 times 9 gives 9 joules.
107924.m: For kinetic energy, the speed is squared first.

107925.q: A cyclist and her bike together weigh 80 kg and travel at 5 m/s. How great is her kinetic energy?
107925.e: ½ times 80 kg times 25 m²/s² gives 40 times 25, which is 1000 joules.
107925.m: Even slow bike rides already have a lot of kinetic energy.

107926.q: A bike with its rider weighs 100 kg and accelerates from standing to 4 m/s. How much kinetic energy does it gain?
107926.e: You calculate ½ times 100 kg times 16 m²/s². That gives 50 times 16, which is 800 joules.
107926.m: Anything that speeds up gains kinetic energy.

107927.q: How does the kinetic energy change if the mass is twice as great but the speed stays the same?
107927.e: The mass is not squared in the formula. Twice the mass therefore gives twice the kinetic energy.
107927.m: Kinetic energy grows in the same proportion as mass.

107928.q: Which has more kinetic energy: a 10 t lorry at 10 m/s or a 1 t car at 20 m/s?
107928.e: Lorry: ½ times 10,000 kg times 100 gives 500,000 J. Car: ½ times 1000 kg times 400 gives 200,000 J.
107928.m: Mass and speed together determine kinetic energy.

107929.q: How much kinetic energy does a football lying still on the grass have?
107929.e: Only an object that is moving has kinetic energy. At a speed of zero, it is zero too.
107929.m: An object at rest has no kinetic energy.

107930.q: How fast must a 1 kg ball fly to have 50 joules of kinetic energy?
107930.e: From ½ times 1 kg times v² equals 50 J, it follows that v² equals 100. The square root of 100 is 10, so 10 m/s.
107930.m: You can work back from kinetic energy to speed.

107931.q: What is meant by elastic energy?
107931.e: When an elastic object is stretched, squeezed or bent, it stores energy. When you let go, it releases it again.
107931.m: Deformed elastic objects store elastic energy.

107932.q: In which of these objects is elastic energy stored?
107932.e: When it is drawn, the bow is bent elastically. When it is released, the elastic energy turns into the kinetic energy of the arrow.
107932.m: A drawn bow stores elastic energy.

107933.q: Which energy conversion happens when a trampoline throws you upwards?
107933.e: When you land, the mat stretches and stores energy. As it springs back, this becomes kinetic energy that carries you upwards.
107933.m: A trampoline gives back stored elastic energy as movement.

107935.q: Which form of energy does the suspension fork of a mountain bike briefly store when the wheel rides over a root?
107935.e: With the jolt, the spring in the fork is compressed and stores energy. Afterwards, it springs back out.
107935.m: A compressed spring stores elastic energy.

107936.q: A stretched rubber band stores 2 joules and fires a paper pellet. What is the most kinetic energy the pellet can get?
107936.e: Energy cannot come from nothing. The pellet can get at most the 2 joules, and some usually turns into heat.
107936.m: Stored elastic energy limits the possible kinetic energy.

107938.q: In pole vaulting, which energy does the strongly bent pole store?
107938.e: The run-up bends the pole strongly, and it stores energy. As it straightens, it releases this energy and lifts the vaulter over the bar.
107938.m: A bent pole stores elastic energy.

a: In the movement of whole objects
In the height of an object
107939.e: In chemical reactions, bonds between atoms are broken and new ones are formed. In the process, energy is released or used.
107939.m: Chemical energy is stored in the bonds of substances.

107940.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a burning candle?
a: Chemical energy into heat and light
107940.e: The wax burns with the oxygen in the air. The chemical energy is released as heat and light.
107940.m: A candle turns chemical energy into heat and light.

107941.q: Which energy conversion takes place when a mobile phone battery is charged?
107941.e: During charging, chemical reactions take place in the battery that store energy. When it is used, they run backwards and supply electricity.
107941.m: A rechargeable battery stores electrical energy in chemical form.

107942.q: Into which forms of energy do muscles turn the chemical energy from food?
107942.e: Muscles use the energy from nutrients to move. A large part of it turns into heat, which is why we get warm when we do sport.
107942.m: Muscles turn food energy into movement and heat.

107943.q: Which energy conversion happens in photosynthesis?
107943.e: Plants use sunlight to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide. The energy is stored chemically in the sugar.
107943.m: Plants store solar energy as chemical energy.

107944.q: Which energy does a petrol engine originally use?
a: The chemical energy of the fuel
The potential energy of the road
The radiant energy of the headlights
The elastic energy of the tyres
107944.e: In the engine, petrol burns with air. The chemical energy released is turned into movement by way of heat.
107944.m: A petrol engine uses the chemical energy of the fuel.

107945.q: What is a chemical reaction called in which energy is released as heat?
107945.e: Exo means out. In an exothermic reaction, heat is given off to the surroundings, for example in burning.

107946.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a torch battery while the torch is shining?
107946.e: Chemical reactions take place in the battery that drive electrons through the circuit. This produces electrical energy.
107946.m: A battery supplies electrical energy from chemical reactions.

107947.q: A 2000-watt hair dryer runs for half an hour. How much electrical energy does it use?
107947.e: Energy is power times time: 2 kW times 0.5 h gives 1 kWh.
107947.m: Electrical energy is power times time.

107948.q: A 2 kW kettle runs for 6 minutes. How much does this cost at 30 centimes per kWh?
107948.e: 6 minutes is 0.1 hours, so it uses 2 kW times 0.1 h, which gives 0.2 kWh. 0.2 times 30 centimes gives 6 centimes.
107948.m: The cost of electricity is calculated as kWh times the price per kWh.

107949.q: How many joules are equal to one kilowatt-hour?
107949.e: 1 kWh is 1000 watts for 3600 seconds. 1000 times 3600 gives 3,600,000 joules.

107950.q: A device on 230 volts draws a current of 2 amperes. What is its power?
107950.e: Electrical power is voltage times current. 230 V times 2 A gives 460 W.
107950.m: Electrical power is voltage times current.

107951.q: A fridge has an average power of 100 watts. How much electrical energy does it use in a day?
107951.e: A day has 24 hours. 0.1 kW times 24 h gives 2.4 kWh.
107951.m: Devices that are always on use a lot of energy over a day.

107952.q: Which of these devices mainly turns electrical energy into heat?
107952.e: In a kettle, current flows through a heating coil, which gets hot. A dynamo, a solar cell and a wind turbine, on the other hand, produce electrical energy.
107952.m: A kettle turns electricity into heat.

107953.q: Which component stores electrical energy directly in an electric field?
107953.e: A capacitor consists of two conducting plates with an insulating layer between them. Energy is stored in the electric field between the charged plates.
107953.m: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field.

107954.q: Why should you switch devices off completely rather than leaving them on standby?
a: On standby they use electricity all the time
On standby they get cold faster
107954.e: Even in standby mode, a small current flows, day and night. Over a year, this adds up to quite a lot of electrical energy.
107954.m: Standby costs electrical energy all the time.

107955.q: What is thermal energy at the level of particles?
a: The kinetic energy of the particles
107955.e: The particles of a substance are always moving. The warmer a substance is, the more vigorously they move.
107955.m: Heat is the movement of the tiniest particles.

107956.q: Which device takes heat from the outside air or the ground and brings it into the house for heating?
107956.e: A heat pump uses electrical energy to bring heat from the cooler surroundings up to a higher temperature. It is very common in new Swiss houses.
107956.m: A heat pump heats with warmth from the surroundings.

107957.q: How does the heat of a campfire reach you when you sit to one side of it?
107957.e: Warm air rises upwards, not sideways. To the side, you mainly feel the fire’s heat radiation.
107957.m: A campfire warms us mainly by radiation.

107958.q: What is it called when a metal spoon in hot tea also gets warm at the handle?
107958.e: The particles in the metal pass their movement on to the neighbouring particles. In this way, the heat travels through the spoon to the handle.

107959.q: How does a radiator spread heat around the whole room?
a: Only by conduction through the floor
107959.e: The air by the radiator gets warm and rises, and cooler air flows in. This creates an air current that warms the room.
107959.m: Warm air rises and spreads the heat around the room.

107960.q: How much energy is needed to heat 2 kg of water by 10 °C (4.2 kJ per kg and °C)?
107960.e: You calculate mass times temperature change times specific heat capacity: 2 times 10 times 4.2 gives 84 kJ.
107960.m: Water needs a lot of energy to get warm.

107961.q: Which substance is pumped through the radiators in many heating systems to carry heat?
107961.e: Water can take up a great deal of heat and is cheap. It carries the heat from the boiler to the radiators.
107961.m: In heating systems, it is usually water that carries the heat.

107962.q: Why do double or triple-glazed windows keep the heat in the house better?
a: The layer between the panes conducts heat poorly
The panes let no light through
107962.e: Between the panes there is air or a noble gas. Gases conduct heat poorly and so slow down heat loss.

107963.q: Why does less solar radiation reach the ground than outside the Earth’s atmosphere?
a: The atmosphere absorbs and scatters some of it
The Sun is further away there
The ground pushes the radiation away
107963.e: Air, clouds and dust absorb some of the solar radiation or deflect it. That is why it is weaker on the ground than in space.
107963.m: The atmosphere holds back some of the solar radiation.

107964.q: What is it called when an object takes in radiation and turns it into heat, for example?
107964.e: To absorb means to take in. The radiant energy passes into the object, which usually warms up.
107964.m: In absorption, an object takes in radiation.

107965.q: Which of the Sun’s rays cause sunburn?
107965.e: UV radiation is high in energy and can damage skin cells. Sun cream and clothing protect against it.

107966.q: Why are emergency blankets shiny and silvery on one side?
a: They reflect the body’s heat radiation back
107966.e: The shiny metal layer reflects a large part of the heat radiation. This means an injured person loses less body heat.

107967.q: What does a solar thermal collector on the roof of a house do?
a: It heats water with solar radiation
107967.e: A liquid flows through the collector and is warmed by the Sun. This heat is used to make hot water or for heating.
107967.m: Solar collectors turn solar radiation into heat.

107968.q: What is the effect called in which gases in the atmosphere hold back some of the Earth’s heat radiation?
107968.e: The Earth radiates heat into space. Gases such as water vapour and methane hold back some of it and so warm the Earth.
107968.m: The greenhouse effect keeps heat in the atmosphere.

107970.q: Which of these surfaces reflects sunlight most strongly?
107970.e: Fresh snow reflects most of the sunlight. That is why you need sunglasses in the mountains in winter.
107970.m: Bright snow reflects a lot of sunlight.

107971.q: In which form is energy mainly released first during nuclear fission in a reactor?
107971.e: The fragments fly apart at high speed and give off their energy as heat to the surrounding water. Only later is this turned into electricity by steam and a turbine.
107971.m: In a reactor, heat is produced first.

107972.q: Which process gives the Sun its energy?
107972.e: In the hot interior of the Sun, light atomic nuclei fuse into heavier ones. This releases enormous amounts of energy.
107972.m: The Sun gets its energy from nuclear fusion.

107973.q: What does the formula E = mc² tell us about nuclear energy?
a: Even a little mass equals a great deal of energy
107973.e: In nuclear reactions, the resulting nuclei together are slightly lighter than the original nuclei. This tiny difference in mass becomes a lot of energy through the huge factor of the speed of light squared.
107973.m: A small mass equals a huge amount of energy.

107974.q: What is the process called in which each nuclear reaction in a reactor itself triggers further reactions of the same kind?
107974.e: Each reaction releases particles that can in turn trigger new reactions. In a reactor, this reaction is controlled so that it runs steadily.
107974.m: A controlled chain reaction takes place in a reactor.

107975.q: What are the control rods in a nuclear reactor for?
107975.e: Control rods contain substances such as boron or cadmium. The deeper they are lowered in, the fewer nuclear reactions take place.
107975.m: A reactor is regulated with the control rods.

107976.q: Which particle splits a uranium nucleus in a reactor?
107976.e: A neutron enters the uranium nucleus and makes it unstable, so that it breaks apart. This releases new neutrons, which can split further nuclei.

107977.q: Where is Switzerland’s highly radioactive waste one day to be stored for ever?
a: In a hall by the railway station
107977.e: Switzerland is planning a repository deep in the rock. There, the waste is to remain safely sealed in for many thousands of years.
107977.m: Radioactive waste is to be stored deep in the rock.

107978.q: Why must radioactive waste be safely sealed in for so long?
a: It keeps giving off radiation for very many years
It can easily explode like petrol
107978.e: Radioactive substances give off dangerous radiation for thousands of years. That is why they must be kept away from people and the environment.
107978.m: Radioactive waste gives off radiation for a very long time.

107979.q: Which unit appears next to kilocalories on food packaging in Switzerland?
107979.e: On packaging, the energy content is given in kilojoules and in kilocalories. The joule is the official unit of energy, named after James Prescott Joule.
107979.m: The energy content of food is given in kilojoules.

107980.q: How much work do you do if you push a box 4 m with a force of 50 N?
107980.e: Work is force times distance: 50 N times 4 m gives 200 newton-metres. One newton-metre is exactly one joule.
107980.m: One joule equals one newton times one metre.

107981.q: Roughly how much energy do you need to lift a 100 g bar of chocolate one metre?
107981.e: A mass of 100 g has a weight of about 1 newton. 1 newton times 1 metre gives about 1 joule.
107981.m: A joule is quite a small amount of energy.

107982.q: How many joules are equal to one watt-second?
107982.e: One watt means one joule per second. A power of 1 watt for 1 second therefore gives exactly 1 joule.
107982.m: One watt-second is exactly one joule.

107983.q: A 10-watt LED lamp shines for one minute. How much energy does it use?
107983.e: Energy is power times time: 10 W times 60 s gives 600 joules.
107983.m: You get joules from watts times seconds.

107984.q: Which physical quantity is not measured in joules?
107984.e: Energy, work and heat all have the unit joule. Power gives energy per unit of time and is measured in watts.
107984.m: Power is measured in watts, energy in joules.

107985.q: What did James Prescott Joule show with his experiments?
a: Mechanical work can be turned into heat
107985.e: Joule used a falling weight to turn a paddle wheel in water. The water warmed up measurably, so work had turned into heat.
107985.m: Work and heat are two forms of the same energy.

107986.e: One megajoule is 1000 kilojoules. 3.6 times 1000 gives 3600 kJ.
107986.m: One megajoule is a thousand kilojoules.

107987.e: One kilojoule is 1000 joules. 2.5 times 1000 gives 2500 joules.
107987.m: To convert kilojoules into joules, you multiply by a thousand.

107988.q: How was a calorie originally defined?
a: Energy to heat 1 g of water by 1 °C
Energy to melt 1 kg of iron
Energy to boil away 1 litre of water
107988.e: The calorie was defined by heating water. One calorie is the heat that warms 1 g of water by 1 °C.
107988.m: One calorie warms one gram of water by one degree.

107989.q: A yoghurt provides 100 kcal. Roughly how many kilojoules is that?
107989.e: You multiply by about 4.2: 100 times 4.2 gives about 420 kJ. Exactly, it is 418.4 kJ.
107989.m: Kilocalories are converted into kilojoules with a factor of 4.2.

107990.q: A glass of milk contains 7 g of protein. How many kilocalories does this protein provide if 1 g of protein provides about 4 kcal?
107990.e: You calculate 7 times 4 kcal. That gives 28 kcal.
107990.m: Energy content is calculated as the amount times the value per gram.

107991.q: What is usually meant when “calories” are mentioned on a packet or in conversation?
107991.e: In everyday life, people often say “calories” but mean kilocalories. One kilocalorie is 1000 calories.
107991.m: In everyday life, calories usually means kilocalories.

107992.q: A snack contains 20 g of fat. Roughly how many kilocalories does this fat provide if 1 g of fat provides 9 kcal?
107992.e: You calculate 20 times 9 kcal. That gives 180 kcal.
107992.m: For energy content, you multiply the amount by the value per gram.

107993.q: Is the calorie a unit of the International System of Units, SI?
a: No, the SI unit is the joule
No, the SI unit is the watt
107993.e: The calorie is an older unit that is not part of the SI. The official unit of energy is the joule.
107993.m: The official unit of energy is the joule, not the calorie.

a: A substance or means that stores energy
107994.e: Energy carriers contain energy that can be used, for example wood, crude oil or electricity. They can be stored or transported.

107995.q: Which of these energy carriers is a fossil fuel?
107995.e: Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from dead living things. They include coal, crude oil and natural gas.
107995.m: Natural gas is a fossil fuel.

107996.q: Which of these energy carriers is a secondary energy carrier?
